The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
19:57:13 UTC
04:57:13 KST

Weeks before the end of the legislative session, some members of Congress are scrambling to reauthorize a controversial warrantless wiretapping authority, possibly by attaching it to a must-pass military spending bill. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD) told Politicothat Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) could be attached to the National Defense Authorization Act. It’s the latest in a grueling fight over a major spying rule that hasn’t technically lapsed.
The clock is running out for America’s most contentious spying law
Warrantless wiretapping proponents are rushing to beat the looming blue wave.
“We don’t have two weeks to work just on FISA,” said Rounds, a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “But if it’s amended onto the NDAA then you can move it forward and get that done in time.”
FISA allows for the warrantless surveillance of certain foreigners’ communications, ostensibly on national security grounds. In part because of FISA’s broad scope, Congress revisits it every few years, both to reauthorize the authority and to reform it. The last effort to do both failed. Despite pressure from President Donald Trump, Congress failed to reauthorize FISA over the summer, in part because leadership wouldn’t allow any amendments — particularly attempts to limit its sweeping scope — to be debated or introduced. (Trump didn’t help matters when he made Bill Pulte the acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, who reportedly bragged about purging one-third of the DNI staff, is now the director of federal housing.) But the surveillance authority didn’t actually lapse because the FISA court rectified surveillance under Section 702 back in March, meaning the surveillance state can keep chugging along as is for another four months.
So why the urgency? If you haven’t heard, there’s about to be a new Congress in town — one that is even less likely to give Trump seemingly unlimited spying powers without some semblance of reform.
Support for — and opposition to — FISA isn’t a clear-cut partisan issue. Last time around, a bipartisan coalition led by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Rep. Jim Himes (D-CT), the ranking member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, led the campaign for a “clean” reauthorization of FISA. Their efforts were defeated largely because of holdouts from the Freedom Caucus, whose privacy concerns echoed those of liberal lawmakers. FISA’s critics wanted reform, not abolition. Their goal was to make it harder for intelligence agencies to use the statute, which is intended for foreign targets, to access Americans’ communications.
“It was remarkable watching two dozen House Republicans stand up to the establishment, stand up to Mike Johnson, and fight to reform FISA,” said Michael Baick, an organizer with the OpenAI boycott campaign QuitGPT, which has been advocating for FISA reform to stop AI surveillance. “This has always been a bipartisan issue where Americans of all stripes can agree, and trying to make deals with the establishment to maintain the status quo, while the ground is shifting, is just short-sighted and missing what this moment really is.”
I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time.
Johnson and Himes were adamantly opposed to any reining in of Section 702, stressing the need for a so-called “clean reauthorization.” Both claimed there had already been reforms. “It ain’t the same FISA,” Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) declared in April.
But the changes reformers most wanted were missing. Among them were a warrant requirement and an end to what critics say are major loopholes. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can pull the communications of non-US persons not in the United States — that is, foreign nationals outside the country. But federal agencies like the FBI and NSA can buy Americans’ data from private brokers, a practice FBI director Kash Patel admits is ongoing. And intelligence agencies can use Section 702 to obtain the communications of non-US persons who are communicating with Americans — a workaround known as the “backdoor search loophole.”
“I think it’s a Hail Mary by surveillance hawks to try to ram through what they wanted to do the entire time,” Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Constitution Project of the Project on Government Oversight, told The Verge. “This is something everyone knew was coming down the pike. There have been months to do this, and I don’t think anyone is saying don’t reauthorize at all. The argument is this is an incredibly powerful surveillance tool, and there needs to be guardrails in place to protect people’s constitutional rights.”
Himes, arguably the Democratic Party’s biggest champion of FISA, seems willing to give Trump one more win before the blue wave crashes down in Washington. “I made it clear to some very senior administration officials that they should get this thing done in the lame-duck,” he told The Hill, “because it’s, you know, going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year.”
But Himes didn’t have the votes this summer, and it’s even less likely that he’ll have the votes for a clean reauthorization now.

The Big Idea: Dan Moren
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
19:51:49 UTC
04:51:49 KST

The Big Idea: Dan Moren
Posted on November 24, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi Leave a Comment
Legality does not equal morality, and author Dan Moren’s band of heisters have got just the charm and questionable ethics to prove it! Hop in your spaceship and follow along in the Big Idea for his newest sci-fi novel, Eternity’s Tomb.
DAN MOREN:
Who among us has not been tempted by the idea of a victimless crime?
On one of our earliest dates, my now wife asked me what felony I’d commit if I could get away with it, and while it may have been attempt to ensure a long and healthy(?) relationship through extortion, my answer was quick enough: an elaborate heist—the kind of elegant, perfectly executed plan where you get away clean and nobody gets hurt.
Alas, I never have pulled off the perfect heist, but the good news is that the next best thing to perpetrating crime is writing about it.
For Z, the protagonist of my new book Eternity’s Tomb, things haven’t really gone to plan. Not so much a career criminal as a career opportunist, Z is just finishing a stint in jail when a floating brain in a jar named Ayex dangles an enticing proposition: recovering a spaceborne tomb that’s been lost for millennia, along with—naturally—all of its riches. Along for the ride are the rest of Z’s former crew: ursine mechanic Graham, genetically engineered murderbird Whistler, and hotshot pilot Trix—who also just happens to be Z’s ex. (It didn’t end well.)
Now, let’s just hang a fedora on it: does the main thread of this plot stem at least in part from my childhood love of classic tomb raids like Indiana Jones? Absolutely. Like any good dungeon crawl, adventures like these pit our band of heroes against devilish traps, labyrinthine tunnels and passages, and more than a few surprises. It’s good old-fashioned pulpy fun.
Right?
See, here’s the thing: the older I’ve gotten, the more I’ve been forced to confront the complexities of those stories. Did those “recovered” pieces really belong in a museum? Was this so-called “archaeology” just out-and-out grave-robbing? What is a tenured professor even doing dodging boulders; shouldn’t he be grading? Is this all being supported by student tuitions?!
So, in the hopes of forging an ethically sustainable adventure plot, I started to concoct a scenario wherein guilt wasn’t a foregone conclusion. What if, I theorized, the tomb in question had been launched from its planet of origin into the stars, on a long and winding path destined for a black hole where it would ultimately be destroyed? What if the civilization that had dispatched it had long since ceased to exist? Who would this really hurt? Moreover, what if said civilization hadn’t just died out, but had instead been wiped out by a planet-level catastrophe? Wouldn’t there be some virtue to recovering its remaining artifacts? (And, you know, liquidating just a meager portion of it as a finder’s fee.)
Suffice it to say, there are no easy answers. I’d set out to write a straightforward adventure story, but ultimately tying myself in narrative knots to avoid the ethical complexities felt like cheating. So rather than duck and dodge the problem like it was a barrage of poison darts triggered by a pressure-sensitive floor, I made the only logical choice: having my characters themselves grapple with the implications.
Granted, this is a crew of thieves and criminals we’re talking about—their moral compass may be a tad off-axis to begin with.
Still, even criminals live by a code. They—unlike globetrotting academics, apparently—have lines they won’t cross. My crew doesn’t see themselves as the bad guys so much as people who just want lives outside of the confines of what society has prescribed for them. Sometimes, for them to survive on those margins, that means bending the rules—but what it doesn’t is mean picking on people who can’t afford it. They’re criminals: they may have lied, stolen, and cheated, but come on—they’re not jerks.
Eternity’s Tomb: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s|Porter Square Books

From CUDA and Jax to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
19:40:43 UTC
04:40:43 KST

From CUDA and JAX to TorchTPU: Lessons from a Cayley Graph Solver
Some time ago, I shared a blog post about working with Cayley graphs, where I solved combinatorial puzzles using AI coding agents, PyTorch on GPUs, and JAX on TPUs. Recently, Google released TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend for TPUs, and I wanted to see how well it works on the same task: whether a PyTorch-native TPU stack could match my A100 training pipeline and my JAX beam search in speed and solution quality, or maybe even beat them.
The short version: getting TorchTPU to work was easy; getting it to work efficiently was considerably harder. My initial training port was 1.65x slower than the A100 implementation, while the first TPU beam search was 5.7x slower than its JAX counterpart.
After optimizing eager execution, rewriting attention, eliminating dynamic tensor shapes, fixing a subtle deduplication bug, and investigating an attention-routing regression, the results changed substantially. Training reached comparable wall-clock performance to the A100, and the optimized TorchTPU beam search became 25% faster per level than JAX on the same eight-chip v6e machine, producing the same total solution length across six test puzzles.
Along the way, the investigation improved the solver itself and resulted in an upstream TorchTPU GitHub issue that led to attention-routing fixes.
The code is available on Kaggle notebooks running on a free TPU v5e-8:
As in the previous post, the code and the experiments were done by coding agents (Claude Code and Codex): I decided what to port, what to measure, and how to judge the results, and they did the implementation and the profiling.
The problem
The CayleyPy Professor Tetraminx competition requires finding the shortest sequence of moves that solves 1000 scrambled puzzles. Formally, it is a shortest-path problem in a Cayley graph (each puzzle state is a node, and each of the 24 possible moves is an edge) with an 88-sticker state.
My solver uses beam search guided by a learned neural heuristic — a 3.4M-parameter PieceTransformer. Instead of treating the 88 stickers individually, it groups them into 50 physical pieces, turns each piece into a token, adds a class token (51 tokens in total), and runs four small transformer layers with eight heads of size 32. At the end, an all-neighbours Q head (a head that predicts, for each of the 24 moves, the distance to solved after that move) outputs 24 numbers. So the beam scores all 24 children of a state with one forward pass on the parent.
For training, the signal is a mix of cheap random walks and exact ground truth:
- Random walks of 2–40 moves from the solved state. A state p moves into a walk has two known labels: undoing the last move gives distance p - 1, and continuing the walk gives p + 1.
- Exact 24-way labels from a breadth-first search (BFS) table at depth 5 or less.
- The puzzle’s 24 spatial symmetries, used as data augmentation.
On the A100, one epoch takes 142.7 seconds. My best checkpoint is epoch 1500 of a 2000-epoch run, about 80 hours in total.
What is TorchTPU
TorchTPU is not PyTorch/XLA: there is no LazyTensor tracing, no xm.mark_step(), and no xla_device(). Instead, TorchTPU lowers ATen ops directly to StableHLO and runs through PJRT and libtpu (PyTorch’s core ops are translated straight into XLA’s input format and executed by the TPU runtime). Once you import torch, "tpu" works as a device string just like "cuda".
It has three execution modes:
- Eager (the default): runs one op at a time asynchronously.
- Fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1): defers ops and fuses them across op boundaries without needing torch.compile.
- Compiled (torch.compile(fn, dynamic=False)): graph compilation targeting the TPU backend.
Three rules matter in practice:
- Static shapes were the reliable path: with the TorchTPU builds and operators I used, fixed tensor shapes and torch.compile(..., dynamic=False) worked best, and every new shape meant a full recompile.
- Data-dependent output sizes were the most expensive: ops like nonzero, masked_select, unique, bincount, and even x[bool_mask] still run in eager mode, but they force a .cpu().item() host round-trip to learn their output size, and a compiled graph gets specialized to that one size, so each new size means another compile.
- Nothing falls back silently to the CPU: an op that TorchTPU doesn’t implement raises an error instead of quietly running slowly.
Part 1: training, from 1.65x slower to 1.08x faster
I ran the first port on a Cloud TPU machine with four v6e chips, using DDP with one process per chip and a global batch of 512, so each epoch saw exactly the same number of samples as on the A100. Before the code could run on the TPU at all, I had to remove four GPU idioms (masked_select in the loss, boolean-mask indexing when expanding labels, 12 .item() metric reads per step, and sampling training anchors on the CPU instead of keeping the 0.19 GB anchor table in TPU memory). This first working version took 234.8 seconds per epoch, 1.65x slower than the A100. I was able to bring it down to 132 seconds with two changes.
Fused eager
The first win was practically free: turning on fused eager (TORCH_TPU_DEFER_AND_FUSE=1). Only the model’s forward and backward pass ran under torch.compile; the rest of the trainer (the random-walk sampler with its 40-iteration loop, label expansion, the loss, and the metrics) ran in eager mode, one op at a time. In default eager mode, that data pipeline took 61.3 ms per step. Wrapping it in torch.compile brought it down to 29.7 ms, while fused eager, which fuses the ops at run time without any code changes, got it to 13.1 ms. The pipeline is many tiny ops, and on this workload they fused better than they compiled; I didn’t profile why, since the cheaper option was also the faster one. Setting that single environment variable dropped the epoch time from 234.8 s to 176.5 s.
The attention rewrite that was almost thrown away
Still, 176.5 s was slower than the A100, and the GPU profile didn’t help. On the A100, the input stage and embedding gradient took 67% of the step; on the TPU, the same stage took only 0.96 ms (0.8%), and the model was spending ~90% of its time in attention.
A roofline at the model’s own shapes explained why. A square 8192³ GEMM hits 361 TFLOP/s on one v6e chip, and the model’s QKV and FFN GEMMs hit 212–259 TFLOP/s, while attention ran at 3.0 TFLOP/s. With T = 51 and head_dim = 32, every attention matmul is 51x32x51 on a 128x128 matrix unit (MXU) — roughly 2.5% tile occupancy. Padding head_dim to 128 or T to 64 actually made things slower (0.83x and 0.81x). As a result, attention is about 3% of the model’s FLOPs but about 90% of its time on the TPU.
If you want to keep the same model (for a fair comparison), you need to keep the same shapes and find other improvements. Standard scaled_dot_product_attention (SDPA) expects (B, H, T, Dh), so the QKV tensor has to be permuted to move the heads to the second dimension. Rewriting attention with torch.einsum keeps the heads in their original dimension and avoids the permutes:
q, k, v = qkv.view(B, T, 3, H, Dh).unbind(2)        # heads never leave dim 2
s = torch.einsum("bthd,bshd->bhts", q, k) * scale
p = s.float().softmax(-1).to(v.dtype)               # fp32 softmax, on purpose
a = torch.einsum("bhts,bshd->bthd", p, v)
The fp32 softmax is there for numerics. On the TPU, the einsum and SDPA versions disagreed by a relative 3.3e-3, so I checked both against a float64 reference on the CPU: both were about 4.6e-3 away from it, because the TPU’s matrix unit uses a single-pass bf16 multiply even for “fp32” matmuls unless you raise torch.tpu.precision. In bf16, keeping only the softmax in fp32 closed the remaining gap between the two versions.
This change was almost rejected. The agent first measured it on the forward pass only, where it looked slower (einsum 5.51 ms vs SDPA 4.56 ms), and discarded it on that basis. Thankfully, I decided to check the full forward+backward pass: the profiler attributed much of the backward-pass overhead to layout conversions around SDPA’s saved tensors, which cost far more than the forward pass saved. Across forward+backward, one layer dropped from 25.14 ms to 14.85 ms (1.69x faster). That pushed the whole epoch down to 132.0 s — 1.08x faster than the A100.
A checkpoint with deadlocks
The most confusing bug was in checkpointing. Saving a checkpoint only from rank 0 is a standard pattern:
if is_main:
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), path)      # deadlocks under fused eager + DDP
Under fused eager, the tensors in state_dict are still deferred. When rank 0 reads them, it executes a graph that includes this step’s DDP collectives, while the other ranks are already waiting at the next barrier. The checkpoint file would grow to 1.1 MB, then 2.2 MB, and freeze forever while every rank sat busy. The fix is to move the tensors to the CPU on every rank and write the file on one:
cpu_state = {k: v.detach().to("cpu") for k, v in model.state_dict().items()}   # all ranks
if is_main:
    torch.save(cpu_state, path)
The trap only fires in the mode that gives the speedup, which made it harder to find.
Summary of training changes
Training results
On Kaggle’s free v5e-8 (eight chips, 64 samples per chip), the training notebook run 186 epochs in 7.41 hours, with a median of 142.4 seconds per epoch against the A100’s 144.2 over the same epochs.
Over epochs 177-186, the training loss averaged 15.131 on the v5e-8 and 15.132 on the A100, and top-1 accuracy was 0.488 against 0.483. On exact labels, the TPU checkpoint at epoch 186 is on par with the A100 checkpoint at epoch 200: its best predicted move is truly optimal for 99.0% of states, against 98.9%. The best checkpoint trained eight times longer and is still better.
Part 2: beam search, first attempt
With training done, the second half was porting my beam search solver (KhoruzhiiSolver, the CUDA beam searcher from the previous post) to TorchTPU. Training needed targeted fixes; the solver needed a rewrite. It relied on torch.unique for deduplication, boolean-mask indexing, and dynamic tensor shapes (cand.index_select(0, unique_pos[:B])), none of which works well on a TPU.
So I wrote beam_tpu.py from scratch in pure PyTorch with fixed shapes across every step. Instead of dropping duplicates, I sort candidates by hash, flag adjacent matches, and assign duplicate scores +inf so topk simply never picks them:
sort_h, sort_idx = h.sort()
dup_sorted = torch.cat([no, sort_h[1:] == sort_h[:-1]])
dup = dup_sorted[sort_idx.argsort()]
score = torch.where(dup | ~valid, BIG, score)
To share a 1M-wide beam across chips, each chip holds an equal share of the beam slots, and a child’s owner chip is determined by its hash. Every step runs the Q-head forward on local parents, routes children to their owners via all_to_all_single, deduplicates globally on each owner, and runs topk for the next level. States are stored as int8, and the tree bookkeeping stays outside the compiled step so the level counter doesn’t trigger a recompilation.
The search doesn’t go all the way to the solved state: it stops as soon as a beam state appears in the exact depth-6 BFS table (27.8M states), and the table supplies the optimal last six moves. In the first TorchTPU version, this endgame tail (a Zobrist hash and a searchsorted over the table for each level, each ending in .item()) ran as eager ops on the TPU and took ~176 s after a 73 s solve. The JAX driver had always done it in NumPy on the host, so I did the same: identical moves on 3000 checked states, at under a millisecond per state. Running the model over fixed-size chunks inside a single scan didn’t change the step speed, but it kept one copy of the model in the compiled graph instead of one per chunk, shrinking the cached compiled code from 363 to 162 MiB.
I first tested an August pre-release of TorchTPU on six hard scrambles (1M beam, 4x v6e). It matched my JAX kernel on path length (186 vs 185 moves, every path replay-verified) but was 5.7x slower (1973 s vs 345 s). The profile showed that cross-chip all_to_all cost only 0.6 ms per step, while model inference took ~83% of the time. Then I moved to the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 on Kaggle, and the results were surprising: the gap narrowed to 2.8x per beam level, but quality dropped, with TorchTPU finding 194 moves where JAX reproduced its 185.
When a backend change exposed an algorithmic bug
Because Kaggle has a long TPU queue, I moved to Cloud TPU v6e to debug the 8 moves lost between the pre-release (186) and 0.2.0 (194). Two things had changed in 0.2.0: torch.topk had reverted from a stable tie-breaking order back to an unstable default, and bf16 attention on sequence lengths that are not a multiple of 128 no longer ran the whole module in fp32 (more on attention below).
On eight v6e chips, forcing the old low-index tie-breaking in topk took 0.2.0 from 193 moves back to 187, the pre-release’s number there. But why should tie-breaking change path length at all? On four chips, every fixed tie order I tried (lowest index first, highest first, a random shuffle) gave 185 moves; only 0.2.0’s native order gave 188. Something in the beam was turning tie order into path length, and that something was my deduplication.
Because the Q head scores children from the parent, a state reached from two parents arrives as two copies with different scores. My dedup sorted candidates by hash and kept the first copy in each run, and since torch.sort is unstable on both builds, “first” was whichever copy the backend left in front. When 0.2.0 changed the tie order, good states started to disappear because their worse duplicate survived. JAX’s dedup uses a stable argsort on score-sorted buckets, so it keeps the better copy.
Replacing “keep first” with a segment-min over (score, index) (so duplicates always keep their best score) added 0.5% overhead and fixed the issue:
On ten more puzzles, this fix cut total moves from 319 down to 302, improving seven of them and worsening none.
Flash attention and the GitHub issue
One regression really was TorchTPU’s: on the same chips, 0.2.0 ran a beam level 1.7x slower than the pre-release. Timing each piece of a level separately showed that everything except attention was as fast or faster in 0.2.0. The cause was routing: 0.2.0 sends short attention shapes to its Flash attention kernel, which pads the 51-token sequence to a 128-token tile, so 84% of each score tile is padding. Turning Flash off with torch.backends.cuda.enable_flash_sdp(False) puts attention back on the plain XLA path (yes, .cuda. — TorchTPU respects PyTorch’s standard SDPA backend switches, which live under torch.backends.cuda):
With Flash off, a full beam level is 4x faster than with 0.2.0’s default and 2.4x faster than the pre-release. The 2026-11-04 nightly, which already routes short sequences away from Flash, is as fast as the workaround.
Two things hid this at first. The --fp32-attn arm that I added to test attention precision still went through Flash, so it only made things slower. And PyTorch’s AOTAutograd cache is keyed on the graph, not on the attention backend flag, so a second process quietly reused the Flash-compiled graph and reported identical times until each run got its own cache directory.
My agent wrote up the measurements and reported the issue to the TorchTPU repository with a Colab reproduction and a table of attention timings across head sizes and sequence lengths. It turned out that the short-sequence fix had already landed on main three days after 0.2.0 was tagged, but it hadn’t been released. The report also noted that a newer routing rule on main would make some 128–256-token shapes slower. The TorchTPU team picked it up, merged a series of attention-routing fixes, and closed the issue on November 21.
Summary of beam search changes
Beam search results
With the dedup fixed and Flash turned off, I reran the comparison on one eight-chip v6e machine with the public torch_tpu==0.2.0 and JAX 0.11.0 (the version in Kaggle’s TPU image).
TorchTPU now runs a beam level 1.25x faster than JAX with the same quality.
On Kaggle’s v5e-8, the picture is closer. TorchTPU with Flash off is still about 10% faster per beam level, but the median scramble takes slightly longer (49.9 vs 48.7 s), because it checks the hit flag only every four levels and runs extra levels, and it found one move more (186 vs 185):
JAX remains my main beam search solution for now as I have yet to run TorchTPU on a wider beam. And the investigations helped push the JAX kernel further: bounding temporary buffers reduced the compile-time memory for a 128M beam from 39.5 to 12 GiB per chip, and a 256M-state beam works on eight v6e chips.
A100 vs TPU: the differences that mattered
Conclusions
I started this experiment to see whether TorchTPU could replace my A100 + JAX setup, and on this task it can: the same model trains at the A100’s speed or slightly faster, and the beam search matches JAX on quality and is a bit faster per level.
However, a native PyTorch API does not eliminate the need for hardware-aware engineering. Static shapes, deferred execution, tensor layouts, compilation caching, and kernel selection all mattered considerably. Optimizations that helped training did not necessarily help inference, and seemingly minor changes in backend behaviour exposed a latent bug in my search algorithm.
The migration also improved both implementations: fixing deduplication reduced solution lengths, the attention investigation contributed to upstream TorchTPU improvements, and revisiting memory management enabled larger beams in JAX.
More broadly, this project demonstrated how AI coding agents can participate in experimental engineering rather than simply code generation. Claude Code and Codex implemented alternative approaches, profiled execution, constructed controlled experiments, investigated regressions, and prepared reproducible bug reports. My role was to formulate hypotheses, choose meaningful metrics, question misleading measurements, and decide which trade-offs were acceptable.

Compiling web applications into verified operations for AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
19:12:02 UTC
04:12:02 KST

Solid-State Web Execution: Compiling Web Applications into Verified Operations for AI Agents
Abstract
A web agent pays a language model to read the page at every step: first to work out what it can do there, then to find out whether its last action worked. Solid-state web execution removes both. On arrival at a page it has never seen, the Protocolis compiler turns the page's controls into typed operations; the model picks one; the compiler runs it, reads the page again and reports what actually changed. Compilation uses no model inference, no site-specific code and no prior visit. To our knowledge it is the first such compiler in operation. We tested it against the browser tools and agents in common use, as shipped, across three model sizes and three task lengths, with its memory and learning switched off. On long tasks that every system attempted, its default mode completed 76 percent (80 of 105); the best alternative in each comparison completed 46 percent. It was the most stable system tested: it never fell below 55 percent in any condition, while every alternative fell to 28 percent or lower. The cheapest alternative on the same model cost 1.9 to 26 times as much per completed task. On a small model it cost less than every alternative on a frontier model, in 30 of 30 pairings, and matched or exceeded its completion rate in 24. When it reported a long task finished, the judge disagreed less than half as often as with the alternatives (22 against 56 percent). Every result is a first visit, the least favourable setting for the design. We publish the tasks, the judging rules and the outcome of all 3,443 counted runs.
Headline results
- On long tasks that every system attempted, its default mode completed 76 percent (80 of 105); the best alternative in each comparison completed 46 percent.
- It was the most stable system tested: it never fell below 55 percent in any condition, while every alternative fell to 28 percent or lower.
- The cheapest alternative on the same model cost 1.9 to 26 times as much per completed task.
- On a small model it cost less than every alternative on a frontier model, in 30 of 30 pairings, and matched or exceeded its completion rate in 24.

What Cloudflare Doesn't Tell You
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
19:03:55 UTC
04:03:55 KST

What Cloudflare Doesn't Tell You
Cloudflare has arguably done more to push modern internet technologies than any other company. The work they have done to enable TLS, IPv6, post quantum encryption, and other modern standards for millions of websites deserves a tremendous amount of credit.
While this is great, Cloudflare also hides many of the shortcomings of the underlying infrastructure from both users and website owners. Yes, you can connect to a Cloudflare website and it'll allow for IPv6, post quantum encryption, and TLS. But Cloudflare's connection to the origin server might be entirely unencrypted and rely exclusively on IPv4. This creates a huge mismatch between what is being presented to users and the reality of the connection.
One of my biggest problems with this is the fact that Cloudflare doesn't do enough to notify website administrators about these issues. While Cloudflare provides tools to inspect these, comprehensive visibility is lacking. The Cloudflare dashboard should notify you about each of these issues where Cloudflare is following better practices than your origin server, without website administrators having to dig through and specifically look for this information. Clear warnings and proactive alerts to administrators would help greatly.
Not only that, but according to Cloudflare's own documentation, they actively prefer IPv4 over IPv6 when making origin server requests, which is particularly disappointing for a company that has done so much to advance IPv6 adoption:
For proxied DNS records that have both an IPv6 and IPv4 origin address, Cloudflare will prefer the IPv4 address when connecting to your origin server.
Even when website administrators invest in deploying IPv6 on their origin servers, Cloudflare still prioritizes IPv4.
I also believe the industry should consider adding functionality so CDNs and other intermediate networks can expose origin TLS connection information alongside their own. This would allow users and network researchers to better understand the encryption state of the entire path and hold website owners accountable for bad security practices. A similar mechanism could expose which IP version is being used to communicate with the origin server.
Cloudflare has an opportunity to not only make modern internet technologies accessible to users, but also encourage adoption of those technologies throughout the underlying infrastructure. Cloudflare should be a catalyst for modernizing the internet, not a mechanism that allows website owners to avoid modernization indefinitely. Improving transparency would be a meaningful step toward achieving that goal.

Google Alternative Kagi Launches An Email Service 9
			
		 	
				Kagi, the company behind the paid Google Search alternative and Orion web browser, has launched a public beta of Kagi Mail, an email service promising "no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in."
"Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once," Kagi says. "There are great ones out there, and we're fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way." On the roadmap, you can expect contacts and an address book in Q1 2027, but native mobile apps aren't expected to arrive until Q3 2027. Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial before you have to pay $99 per year. The service is available as part of a $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription.

Iran's quest for its own Monroe Doctrine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:58:59 UTC
03:58:59 KST

Iran’s quest for its own Monroe Doctrine
- November 24, 2026
- Meir Javedanfar
- Themes: Geopolitics, Iran, Middle East
The Islamic Republic aims to drive the United States from the Middle East – and then assert its regional supremacy.
President Trump is looking for a new nuclear deal with Iran. But what the leadership of the Islamic Republic of Iran is looking for is something beyond that: its own version of the Monroe Doctrine.
Outlined in 1823 by President James Monroe, the doctrine asserted that the United States would not accept any new European colonisation or military intervention in the Americas. Today, Iran wants an equivalent agreement, one that declares the Middle East ‌off limits to American forces. This is why the withdrawal of US troops from the Middle East, which Iran refers to as ‘West Asia’, has been one of Iran’s preconditions for an agreement. Iran uses this term to refer to the Middle East because it sees the latter as a Eurocentric definition, created by the imperialist powers.
The leadership of the Islamic Republic sees the current conflict as an unmissable opportunity to establish a new sphere of influence for itself in the region. Powerful figures, such as Rezaei and Ali Akbar Velayati, adviser to Iran’s supreme leader on international affairs, call this the ‘emerging West Asian order’. In this new order, the US will no longer have any bases in the region, while any new regional arrangement must include Iran’s concerns and considerations.
Fulfilling this goal will not be easy and Iran’s leadership realises this; accordingly, it has moved beyond rhetoric towards action to fulfil its ambition, pursuing a two-pronged strategy.
First, it has attacked regional countries that host American military bases on their soil. This is why Iran has targeted all the Arab Gulf states and Jordan during the recent war. Iran hopes that this will force the host countries to view these bases on their soil as a liability, and conclude that US bases attract insecurity and conflict, rather than security and stability. As the speaker of Iran’s Parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, stated in May this year: ‘some governments in the region believe that the presence of America will bring them security. But recent events [i.e. attacks against US bases in Gulf countries] have illustrated that such a presence does not create security, rather, it creates insecurity for them’.
Second, it has sought to establish control over the Strait of Hormuz through attacks against ships that wish to pass through it without Iran’s permission. This is in addition to insisting that Iran retains control over this important waterway as part of a future agreement with the US. The Strait is a vital economic artery for the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Controlling it gives Tehran immense leverage to pressure these nations into downgrading or expelling American forces.
This strategy risks pushing the Gulf countries further towards the US. However, Iran believes that, ultimately, these countries will reach the conclusion that Washington is an unreliable partner. Just as it abandoned Afghanistan and left its Kurdish allies in Syria high and dry, it will also abandon its Persian Gulf partners for the simple reason that it does not have the stomach or incentive to pursue a prolonged conflict far away from its own borders.
One of the key challenges faced by the Monroe Doctrine was enforcement. On numerous occasions, European powers defied the doctrine by intervening militarily in the Americas, including Britain seizing the Falkland Islands in 1833 and the French intervention in Mexico in 1861. Originally underwritten by British naval supremacy, Washington’s claims over the Western Hemisphere were only truly enforced when the United States emerged as a major military and naval power during the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
By insisting on formal control over the Strait of Hormuz as part of a final deal with Washington, Iran wants to ensure that, unlike with the original Monroe Doctrine, it has the means to enforce its own version. The Islamic Republic’s missile and drone arsenal, generated by the regime’s domestic production capabilities, have already inflicted heavy military and economic costs on its adversaries. Securing total control over the Strait, backed by Iran’s armed forces, would provide Tehran with credible deterrence against both foreign powers seeking to deploy forces to the region and regional states that consider hosting them.
Iran’s current strategy has been shaped by several developments since 7 October 2023, many of which have been against Iran’s interests. Chief among them has been the weakening of Iran’s ‘Axis of Resistance’. This has been through the loss of the Assad regime in Syria, and Iran’s Hamas and Hezbollah allies becoming militarily weakened. Iran believes that the best time to compensate for these losses is now by using the leverage afforded by its hold over Hormuz and attacks against Persian Gulf countries.
The emphatic defeat suffered by President Trump’s Republican Party in the US midterm elections has emboldened Iran’s decision-makers. The Islamic Republic’s leaders believe that the American people have shown that they are unwilling to pay the price of war against Iran, owing to the costs imposed by Iran through attacks against oil and gas installations and transport networks, which have driven up the price of energy. As the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, General Rezaei stated the day after the midterms, ‘the great people of Iran imposed a strategic defeat on the US on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz, and a political defeat against Trump’.
The Iranian leadership’s resolve is further strengthened by the belief that a US departure from the region would strengthen its standing at home, allowing the regime to present itself as victorious in its conflict against a mighty foe and vindicating its claim to be the region’s greatest power. Ultimately, the Islamic Republic wants the Trump administration to recognise it as the main power in the Middle East, just as it has recognised China as the superpower of the Far East, and Russia as a major European regional power. The regime’s leaders believe that Iran deserves a seat at the table of great powers and should be invited to diplomatic conferences, such as the trilateral summit between Xi, Putin and Trump that took place on 19 November in China. They do not expect their Russian and Chinese allies to negotiate on their behalf.
History has taught Iran’s leaders that despite warm words of friendship, the leaders of China and Russia put their own interests above those of Iran. They are even willing to use their influence over Iran as a bargaining chip in their dealings with the US at Iran’s expense.
The leadership of the Islamic Republic regards the ongoing war as a convergence of opportunities that must be leveraged to reshape the regional balance of power in its favour. To do so, it needs to push the US out, and to make sure it stays out. The leverage it has gained through recent events is one it believes it can use to redraw the map of the region, assert local supremacy, and exclude hostile foreign forces. In short, it wants to secure for itself in the Middle East what President Monroe proclaimed for the United States in the Western Hemisphere in 1823.

Corollary 1.2 transfers the bound to the directed Hamiltonian cycle polynomial
over every field and to the permanent outside characteristic two.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:44:57 UTC
03:44:57 KST

Mozilla released Firefox 161 on Tuesday with a new setting you can use to choose which pages automatically open with the browser’s VPN active. Using the “Manage VPN rules” option in Firefox’s VPN panel, you can set it to “always on” or “always off” for specific sites, so you don’t have to toggle it manually every time you visit certain pages.
Now Firefox can select which sites use its VPN, and clear your browsing history with one click
The new ‘Fire’ button can wipe history, cookies, and other data right from your toolbar.
Starting Tuesday, Mozilla is also rolling out a “Fire” button in standard Firefox windows that lets you quickly clear your browsing data directly from the toolbar. You can choose which data it deletes, including browsing history, downloads history, cookie data, site data, temporary files, saved form info, and website permissions and preferences. If you set the button to delete all of that data, clicking it will sign you out of everything and open a fresh Firefox window.
Tuesday’s Firefox update also adds an option for creating a keyboard shortcut for copying your current tab’s URL, and brings its “read aloud” option in Reader Mode to the Android version of Firefox. Alongside the update, Mozilla says Firefox is also now available directly through the Play Store on cars with Google built-in.

Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups

2026-11-24
18:30:42 UTC
03:30:42 KST

Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.
Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.
The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.
The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.
Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.

A Day in the Life of a Senior Leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:28:20 UTC
03:28:20 KST

One of many unexpected benefits of Ask Rands is that having a robot answer questions from the internet about all of your writing helps you discover contradictions. I’ve flip-flopped on whether a leader should code, and Grumbles knows this and explains it:
Yes, and he did it out loud. In “Technicality” (2007), Rands lays out his old new-manager rule, “Stop coding,” then says: “Too bad I’m wrong.” He adds, “Not totally,” and jokes he might need to call past co-workers to apologize. That’s not a flip-flop so much as a signed confession.
Another evolution. I stopped using the word managers and started using the word leaders. This is problematic, as the book most folks know is called “Managing Humans.” Gotta say it — love that punchy title, but how does that square with one of my favorite pithy sayings: “Managers tell you where you are. Leaders tell you where you are going”?
So, which is it, Rands? Leaders or managers?
Wait for it.
The End of the Trilogy
I’m delighted (relieved) to report that I wrote another book. I’m calling it the end of the trilogy because the first O’Reilly book, Software Developer’s Career Handbook, focuses on getting into leadership; the second one, The Art of Leadership, worked on second-level managers often known as Directors, and this one focuses on a day in the life of the senior leaders, the Executives.
There was no grand plan to do a trilogy. The writing mostly comes from this blog, and over the years that I wrote, I was a front-line manager, a Director, and an Executive. The writing reflects the experience.
A Day in the Life contains the most original writing of any of the books, including original sections for your Morning, Afternoon, Evening, and Night. I had a large amount of help from Grumbles, who wrote none of the words, but was incredibly handy with technical and organizational issues. Thanks, Grumbles!
I’d also like to thank Charity Majors, who wrote the foreword for this book; my favorite line:
Stories train the LLM between your ears.
It’s Both
If you read my pithy saying as a ding on managers, you’re right. That was the original intent. At the time, I was frustrated with the managers who just managed. Just told me where we were. Assessed the current situation. And didn’t seem to care about the future. Leadership, the act of imagining a better future and figuring out how to get there, seemed much more relevant and helpful.
It’s both. There are times when you need to manage and an equal number of times when you need to lead. A great manager is who I need to be when the sky is starting to fall. This is a human who knows how to handle the disaster. They aren’t going to prevent it, but that’s work for later when everyone has calmed down.
And then there are times we require a great leader. Close your eyes and imagine a leader you admire. Tell me a story about them. I bet you have a story about an awe-inspiring accomplishment or perhaps a product they built. Or advice they gave you at just the right time.
These impressive leaders — they are just humans… like you. What they do differently is that they’ve built a set of habits that give them time, space, and tools to lead. This book is not about grand accomplishments; it’s about how to find that time, build that space, and refine the tools.

“Pervert glasses" named word of the year by Macquarie Dictionary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:21:01 UTC
03:21:01 KST

Each year, the Macquarie Dictionary calls together a select Committee to discuss the new words and definitions that have entered the Macquarie Dictionary over the past year. The aim of this is to select one of these to be awarded the Committee’s Choice Word of the Year.
As part of this process, our editors create a longlist of words across 13 categories which, over the course of a few hours, are whittled down into a shortlist. And from this, the Word of the Year is chosen.
The Committee this year was comprised of:
- Editorial Team at Macquarie Dictionary
- David Astle – crossword maker, radio host, and writer
- Tiger Webb – language research specialist, ABC
The shortlist is then opened to the public to register what you think the Word of the Year should be. The word with the most votes is awarded the People’s Choice Word of the Year.
You can review the final shortlist here (and for those interested, the longlist here). Thank you for helping us decide on the defining new word of 2026!
Macquarie Dictionary Word of the Year 2026
2026 has undeniably been another year of rapid technological development, especially in the world of AI, as it finds its way into more and more parts of our lives. This year’s Word of the Year winner and runners up reflect this continued development, but also recognise that life does continue in and around our changing world.
Committee Winner
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
‘The coinage pervert glasses is a succinct reflection of the state of the world in 2026 in so many ways. On the one hand, we’ve seen a massive acceleration in the capabilities of AI and products that integrate it. At the same time, the undeniably critical nickname pervert glasses mirrors the widespread calls to hit the brakes on this seemingly unchecked development. The name represents the year we’ve all endured, with AI, the manosphere, increasing surveillance in supermarkets, and more. Sure these new gadgets might be marketed as smart glasses or camera glasses, but it seems to us that pervert glasses paints a more apt reflection of the year.’
–THE COMMITTEE
Committee Honourable Mentions
PMOS
noun (polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome) a disorder, possibly genetic, leading to irregularities in ovulation and menstruation in women; associated with acne, excess hair growth, insulin resistance, and obesity. Formerly known as PCOS (polycystic ovarian syndrome).
‘As awareness of medical misogyny (a WOTY 2025 honourable mention) spreads, we hope to see more terms like PMOS entering the dictionary. It shows the power that language can hold, both negatively in the problems caused by the commonly misleading term PCOS, and positively in how this decade-long Australian-led campaign to rename this condition was recently adopted worldwide.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AGENTIC
adjective (especially of artificial intelligence) able to act or make decisions independently.
‘While it might not be the most flashy, funny, or socially impactful word on the surface, agentic has seen an exponential increase in usage over the last 12 months. Where 2024 and 2025 saw the development and massive spread of large language models, the release of agentic AI tools such as OpenClaw and the mischief they recently wrought has brought this otherwise very technical term firmly into the mainstream.’
–THE COMMITTEE
MARRICKVILLE PAUSE
noun Colloquial a temporary halt in conversation by people in the inner-west suburbs of Sydney, to await the passing of a loud, low-flying aircraft, after which the conversation continues.
[so called because the suburb Marrickville lies directly beneath a flight path, in very close proximity to the international airport]
‘It is undeniable that we are facing major cultural shifts in the digital world, and as a result, seeing huge language innovation at an international scale. Marrickville pause represents a departure from this trend – a highly localised term for a purely physical phenomenon, but one that is so universally experienced by people who spend time in the area.’
–THE COMMITTEE
People’s Choice Winner
And we have a threepeat! For the third year running, the public have aligned with the Committee’s choice by selecting pervert glasses to be crowned People’s Choice Word of the Year 2026!
PERVERT GLASSES
plural noun Colloquial camera glasses; smart glasses.
[from the use by some of filming or taking photos of others without their knowledge or consent]
People’s Choice Honourable Mentions
DIGITAL DEMENTIA
noun a supposed condition characterised by short-term memory loss, attention deficit, impaired decision-making, etc., thought to result from an excessive reliance on digital devices and artificial intelligence.
‘Digital dementia is, of course, not a real medical diagnosis but that hasn’t stopped the fear of an increasing reliance on digital devices from resonating deeply. People are finding that they’re struggling to navigate without Google Maps and to make and remember plans without iCal. It will be interesting to see if all of this outsourcing does in fact lead to impaired cognition in the long term.’
–THE COMMITTEE
AI;DR
interjection Colloquial a term used by a reader to indicate to others that an online item has been created by AI and is not worth reading.
[AI + d(on’t) or d(idn’t) r(ead); modelled on TL;DR]
‘A nice play on TL;DR (a code for too long; didn’t read), AI;DR gives fellow readers an instant heads-up that the text to follow is what they consider to be AI slop. As the sheer volume of AI generated text is ever-increasing, this succinct code will become a much-welcomed time saver.’
–THE COMMITTEE

David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:12:33 UTC
03:12:33 KST

Though David Fincher’s fans had been eagerly anticipating The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, early screenings of the Once Upon a Time in Hollywood sequel starring Brad Pitt have raised questions about whether generative AI was used in the film. People have claimed that the movie is chock-full of uncanny, inconsistent visuals that make it feel more like slop than the sort of polished film you’d expect from the director of sleek productions like Fight Club and The Social Network.
David Fincher is being dragged for suspected use of AI in his latest film
Early screenings of David Fincher’s latest film are raising questions about whether the director used generative AI.
Following a number of Cliff Booth critics screenings that took place last week ahead of the film’s premiere on November 25th, moviegoers rushed to social media to lament what they saw. One of the most vocal reactions came from YouTuber / director Patrick Tomasso, who said on X that he walked out of his screening feeling “completely gutted” and that the film featured “some of the most blatant and egregious AI use” he has ever seen from a major studio. Tomasso also insisted you can see AI-generated footage in Cliff Booth’s trailers that have been posted online, and he was confident that Fincher’s latest film is filled with “slop as you know and loathe it. The shit you can pump out of Higgsfield.”
Others echoed Tomasso’s sentiments, writing that “the amount of AI in the CLIFF BOOTH movie is astounding to an absurd degree” and vowing to “never watch another Fincher, Pitt or Tarintino [sic] movie again.” Yet some critics enjoyed the film and suggested that the bad AI people thought they were seeing might have actually just been bad CGI. Netflix has neither confirmed nor denied whether AI was used in any capacity to make the film, but Netflix’s heavy involvement in the film’s production and the company’s recent investments in generative AI technology left many suspicious.
It did not help that David Fincher, in a recent interview with the Los Angeles Times, responded to questions about his thoughts on AI with “I’m not a Luddite, so I don’t fear the unknown.” Fincher also reasoned that the anti-AI crowd is advocating for artists to stop iterating on their creative processes: “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid? How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?” The spiel made it sound like he might be jumping on the AI bandwagon.
Set about a decade after Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, Cliff Booth picks up in 1977 at a time when Booth (Pitt) has left his life as a stuntman behind to become a fixer who quietly deals with scandalous problems for Hollywood elites. Cliff still works a number of side gigs as a projectionist and bartender. But the movie is primarily focused on his budding romance with critic-turned-talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki) and his working relationship with Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), a TV actor who needs Booth’s services to keep his wife (Carla Gugino) from being murdered.
At least one trailer for the film features some baffling shots of what looks like people sitting backward in a horse-drawn carriage that make it seem like there might be some generative AI in the mix. It’s hard to tell from the trailers whether that’s actually the case, but in a moment when many creators have been trying to pass off AI generations as human-made art, it’s not surprising that people are suspicious.
Netflix has been incorporating AI into its movies and series for some time now, and it seemed like the company was doubling down earlier this year when it acquired Ben Affleck’s startup, InterPositive, for around $600 million. Rather than turning text into visual outputs like many commercially available AI tools, InterPositive’s AI models are designed to generate assets based on footage captured during a film’s production. According to Netflix, InterPositive’s AI was developed with the intention of making it easier to tweak details like lighting or to remove unwanted background elements. The company also made a big deal of emphasizing that InterPositive’s models were highly customizable and well suited to replicating a human director’s signature style.
Netflix buying InterPositive and absorbing the company’s development team is part of why there has been so much speculation about AI being used in Cliff Booth. If Cliff Booth actually uses AI and the visuals really are as bad as some have said, it would be a major knock against both Netflix and Fincher — a director known for his meticulous (obsessive, some might argue) attention to detail.

UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
18:02:59 UTC
03:02:59 KST

The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.
The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.
The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.
The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.
While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.
“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.
The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.
The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”
The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

Mayo Clinic To Give Appointment Workers 5 Paid Minutes a Day To Boot Up Computers (cbsnews.com) 34
			
		 	
				Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay more than $906,000 in back wages to employees who schedule patient appointments. An investigation by Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison found that employees were performing unpaid work before and after their shifts, including time spent booting up computers and finishing patient calls. Under the settlement (PDF), Mayo will stop rounding employees' work hours and give them five paid minutes at the start of each shift to boot up their computers. CBS News reports:  In a statement, Mayo Clinic said it reached the agreement to resolve concerns about "certain timekeeping practices" involving a group of the specialists. The clinic said it doesn't agree with the attorney general's position but decided that a resolution in which money went to its staff, rather than to defense fees, was preferable. Mayo said it is committed to paying employees accurately and appropriately and reviews its compensation policies regularly. Neither the announcement nor the statement says how many workers are covered or how far back the unpaid time goes.
"Under Minnesota law, workers need to be compensated for all the time they work," Ellison said. State law requires employers to pay employees for all time spent on duties connected to their jobs, including time on the employer's premises. Ellison said Mayo cooperated with the investigation and changed its policies on its own to pay workers for the time. He said other employers should take note: "they're on the clock and need to be paid" if they are on site or doing work duties. Ellison encouraged any worker who believes they're being underpaid to contact his office, saying it may be able to help co-workers as well.

Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:44:34 UTC
02:44:34 KST

It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.
While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.
The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.
In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.
The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.
Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

Electric truck startup Harbinger gets financing boost from Palmer Luckey’s bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:29:09 UTC
02:29:09 KST

Harbinger has tapped Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank as a new source of capital as the electric truck startup looks to diversify how it funds its growth and an expanding portfolio of products spanning autonomous vehicles, energy storage, and defense.
Los Angeles-based Harbinger said Tuesday it secured more than $100 million in financing, including a convertible note from Pinegrove Venture Partners and senior debt from Erebor Bank, which launched in February 2026 and recently surpassed $1 billion in loans, according to the Financial Times.
The new financing comes less than three weeks after Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D funding round co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. FedEx, which ordered 2,000 trucks from Harbinger, also participated.
Harbinger co-founder and chief executive John Harris explained in a statement that building an industrial technology company at scale requires a “different financing approach,” adding that the capital needed to ramp up production and deliver vehicles to customers shouldn’t have to come entirely from equity. Harris noted that major vehicle and aerospace manufacturers have long relied on debt financing to support their production operations.
Erebor is now Harbinger’s primary banking partner. In a statement, Luckey said traditional lenders have struggled to support the unique capital needs of businesses developing real technology and creating U.S. jobs.
“Harbinger is exactly the kind of business we built Erebor to back: an American manufacturer building world-class technology,” he said.

Matic robot vacuum

Narwal Flow 2

Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone

Switchbot K11 Plus

Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:17:09 UTC
02:17:09 KST

Tidal is officially banning AI-generated music on December 9th. As a result of this change, Tidal will delete around 29 million AI-generated songs and reject an estimated 80,000 to 85,000 tracks per day, according to Tidal music lead Robert Andersen.
Tidal will start banning AI-generated music next month
The music streaming platform estimates that it will delete 29 million songs as a result of the AI ban.
The move comes just months after Tidal began labeling and demonetizing tracks identified as 100 percent AI-generated. In a post on X, Andersen says Tidal needed to take a more “drastic” measure, as AI music made up 43 percent of the tracks distributed to the platform in the last 90 days. “We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96% of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all,” Andersen adds.
Bandcamp similarly banned AI music earlier this year, while other music streaming platforms attempt to address a flood of AI songs by applying new labels or removing them from user algorithms. Spotify recently announced that it removed 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from recommendations over the past year, and also launched new “AI persona” badges for artists that use an AI identity. YouTube has rolled out AI music labels as well, while Apple Music is planning to launch AI labels this year. Meanwhile, Deezer is giving users the option to filter out AI music.
“Wholly AI-generated music intended to mislead listeners and impersonate artists is another serious problem that has only increased in scale: It diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans,” Tidal says in a separate post on X.
The platform is also going to ban music distributors from submitting AI songs, using the AI detection tool Ircam Amplify and metadata checks to reject submissions generated solely with AI. Tidal notes that it won’t ban songs made with the assistance of AI tools, as long as AI doesn’t make up the “sole output.”

Top MIT Physicist: Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About 'Taking over the World'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:10:45 UTC
02:10:45 KST

Anthropic Staff Openly Talk About ‘Taking Over the World’, Claims Top MIT Physicist
Apparently they discuss overthrowing the US government after a few drinks.
by Clare Hymer
24 November 2026
Employees at US artificial intelligence company Anthropic openly talk about “overthrowing the US government” and “taking over the world”, a world-renowned physicist has claimed.
In an interview with Novara Media, Max Tegmark, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said: “When I talk to people who work for Anthropic, after they’ve had a couple of drinks, the conversation often gets into overthrowing the US government and taking over the world.”
“They tend to not use words like ‘coup’ and ‘overthrow the US government’. They instead use the code phrase ‘alignment without control’,” he said.
‘Alignment without control’ is the idea that AI should be kept in check by being instilled with certain values – likely those shared by Anthropic, Tegmark said – rather than being directly controlled by humans.
“We get the sort of future that Alan Turing predicted, where it’s going to be Anthropic’s machine-god running Earth, and then the rest of us just have to hope that somehow it’s gonna be nice.”
Turing, widely regarded as the founder of computer science, famously warned in 1951 that once machines started thinking, we should expect them to take control.
Tegmark said the comments from Anthropic staff should alarm anyone who cares about democracy. “These companies really don’t seem to like it [democracy]. They have lobbied really hard to even prevent any meaningful government oversight of them,” he said.
He added: “Here in the US, OpenAI and Anthropic are less regulated than a sandwich shop.”
Novara Media has approached Anthropic for comment.
Tegmark’s disclosure comes as protests against AI are ramping up across the world.
As Anthropic started trading on the stock market at a staggering $2tn valuation on Thursday, protesters gathered at both the Nasdaq exchange in New York and the firm’s San Francisco headquarters demanding an AI development slowdown.
On Saturday, over 1,000 people marched against “AI extinction” in London in what campaigners said was “the biggest AI safety march in history”.
Clare Hymer is head of articles at Novara Media.

Meta brings its Muse AI assistant directly into Instagram DMs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.
The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.
Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.
Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.
Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.
Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.
Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.
Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

GTA 6 Hacker Released On License With Warning 'Don't Let This Happen Again' (bbc.com) 27

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week. He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5 million to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time. The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman -- a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.

Tidal to ban and remove millions of AI-generated tracks as AI slop inundates music streaming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:46:00 UTC
01:46:00 KST

Music streaming service Tidal said on Tuesday that it will start banning and removing songs generated fully with AI in a bid to stem the flood of submissions to its platform. The company said that over the past 90 days, more than 43% of tracks uploaded to its platform were generated by AI, and that was a major reason driving this decision.
Tidal said it will start removing fully AI-generated music on December 9, and the process will result in more than 29 million songs being deleted from the platform by the end of the year. With the new rules in place, the platform said it will be rejecting roughly 80,000-85,000 tracks per day.
Tidal is also banning distribution services from delivering 100% AI-generated tracks, and will reject submissions if songs’ metadata says they are made fully using AI.
The company said it will still accept songs that were made with AI assistance, but not fully generated.
The move comes as AI-generated music inundates streaming services across the board. Tidal is one of the first major platforms after Bandcamp to ban AI music outright. Deezer, which also provides detection tools to other streaming services, said that it will introduce a toggle to let users filter out AI music. Larger platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music have adopted a milder approach to this issue, choosing to label AI-generated music instead of offering filters or taking stronger measures.
Tidal started de-monetizing songs made using AI in June, but that did not prove enough of a deterrent, Tidal Music’s lead, Robert Anderson, said on X.
The company said that 27 million, or 6.3% of tracks on the platform, are fully AI-generated, but 96% of those have no streams.
“It’s true that not all songs catch on immediately, and artists should have time to build their fanbases. But this situation is different – at this scale, the authentic music and artists that Tidal subscribers are looking to listen to and discover get buried,” the company said in a post.
Meanwhile, music labels are trying to make money by partnering with platforms and AI model makers to sell their catalog for training or remixing features. Goldman Sachs estimates that by 2035, AI-related licensing tools and new monetization opportunities have the potential to improve record labels’ revenue by 10%.

Uber and Nuro begin driverless testing of Lucid robotaxis ahead of 2027 launch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:40:46 UTC
01:40:46 KST

Uber and Nuro have started testing driverless Lucid Gravity SUVs on public streets in the San Francisco Bay Area more than six months after receiving the permit that allowed the companies to pull the human safety driver from behind the wheel.
The companies will soon begin offering driverless rides to employees in the final lead-up to launching a commercial robotaxi service in the first quarter of 2027.
The milestone comes just 16 months after Uber announced an ambitious plan to launch a premium robotaxi service using Lucid electric vehicles outfitted with autonomous vehicle technology developed by startup Nuro.
That plan came with hefty investments in both companies and much-needed endorsements of their respective products. Uber initially agreed to invest $300 million in Lucid — a figure that has since ballooned to $500 million. Uber also agreed to invest nearly $500 million in Nuro, TechCrunch previously reported, citing sources familiar with the deal.
The agreement provided both Lucid and Nuro with boosts beyond the obvious capital injection. Uber agreed to buy at least 20,000 of Lucid Gravity SUVs over the next six years, giving the struggling EV maker a more predictable source of revenue. Nuro, meanwhile, was less than a year removed from announcing a risky, but necessary pivot away from developing driverless delivery vehicles and toward licensing its autonomous vehicle technology to automakers and mobility companies.
Nuro has spent nearly a year testing the Lucid Gravity robotaxi on public roads in the San Francisco Bay Area with a human safety operator behind the wheel. The California Department of Motor Vehicles, the agency that regulates the testing and deployment of autonomous vehicles in the state, granted Nuro a driverless AV permit in May 2026.
Uber and Nuro are also testing autonomous vehicles on public roads in Houston with human safety operators behind the wheel. Nuro is supplementing that on-road testing with closed-course testing and simulation to validate the self-driving system before opening the robotaxis to the public. The companies’ combined engineering fleet of autonomous vehicles, which stood at 100 AVs earlier this year, is expanding as Lucid begins manufacturing the first production versions of the robotaxis at its Arizona factory.
The Lucid Gravity robotaxi, unveiled in January 2026, is outfitted with high-resolution cameras, solid-state lidar sensors, and radars that help the self-driving system perceive the real-world environment and operate in it. Uber, which will own and operate the fleet, has focused its efforts on the in-cabin experience, including how riders will interact with the vehicle.
