Why a Crusoe investor is betting on solar and batteries to power future AI data centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:10:00 UTC
01:10:00 KST

The problem of supplying power to AI data centers has become one of the central debates of the AI era. In just a few years, the U.S. grid has gone from basically zero growth to adding several gigawatts a year.
“Demand is growing faster than people appreciate,” Brook Porter, partner at G2 Venture Partners (G2VP), told TechCrunch. “It’s atoms, not bits, and the world is in the process of recognizing the realities of those challenges.”
It’s been a bumpy road. Because it takes a while to scale supply chains, companies have been securing power in any form they can. In many cases, that has meant buying, renting, and deploying natural gas power plants, but Porter thinks that hyperscalers and data center developers should look at the bigger picture if they want to move faster.
That picture involves solar paired with energy storage, based on an analysis Porter and his colleagues at G2VP recently conducted on the state of the data center power market.
“Global capacity of natural gas is only about 60 or 70 gigawatts per year, where solar is already at well over a terawatt,” he said. “Probably the most important lesson that we’ve learned over the last 20 years of backing companies is that Wright’s Law is the thing you want to leverage — making the same thing over and over again.”
Both solar and most forms of long-duration energy storage are built on small, modular technologies that can be manufactured at massive scale. “This is about speed and scale and economics, and we can win across all those dimensions,” Porter said.
G2VP had an early window into AI data center development, having led Crusoe’s Series C. “We’ve had a front-row seat at what’s been happening at that company, how they’ve evolved, how the different waves of data centers have evolved,” Porter said.
The venture firm estimates that data center investment will top $4 trillion until the end of the decade. As the next wave takes shape, the firm sees two different paths for data centers: small, on-grid facilities with their own generating capacity, and larger data centers powered by solar and long-duration energy storage.
“The big idea is to go off-grid,” Porter said. “What that would enable you to do is build with renewables in a way that’s independent of the grid. You can determine your own fate, go around some of the constraints of permitting, whether that’s access to the grid or air permits. You can accelerate your time to market dramatically.”
In recent years, energy storage has been synonymous with lithium-ion batteries, which are too expensive to compete with fossil fuels for round-the-clock power. But a new generation of long-duration energy storage products from the likes of Form Energy and G2VP portfolio company Antora Energy have brought the cost per megawatt-hour down significantly.
Even though the technologies might be a few years away from broad acceptance among data center developers, Porter said they should start thinking about them now.
“It’s analogous to surfing the biggest waves off of Mavericks here in Northern California. The wave is so big that you really have to be paddling and moving and be incredibly nimble to catch it. If you’re at a standstill, it’s just gonna blow you by,” he said.

The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

Pinterest will now let parents limit the AI-generated content their teens see
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:02:37 UTC
01:02:37 KST

Pinterest announced this week that it’s expanding its parental controls, but one new feature stands out: Parents can now control how much AI-generated content their children are exposed to. This additional setting arrives alongside more standard options, like tools to adjust notifications or whether or not videos auto-play.
The change makes Pinterest one of the first major social platforms to allow parents to control how much AI-generated content is shown to their children as part of the overall user experience.
Aside from Pinterest, social media platforms have focused more on limiting minors’ access to specific AI-powered features, as when Snap added a parental control setting that prevented its AI chatbot from responding to teens or when Meta announced a global pause on teens’ access to existing AI characters after retooling the product based on parents’ feedback.
WhatsApp currently allows parents to adjust the level of access teens have to Meta AI, in terms of using AI to create content or having the AI respond to their teen’s questions.
But when it comes to AI-generated content filling users’ feeds and recommendations, there are few controls available on social media platforms in general, much less those provided as part of the parental controls.
This problem, parents say, is harming children’s well-being in favor of profits. For instance, in April, the children’s advocacy group Fairplay sent a letter to YouTube CEO Neal Mohan and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, signed by over 200 organizations and experts, calling on YouTube to remove AI-generated content from YouTube Kids and bar AI-generated videos from being recommended to users under 18.
Pinterest has fought its own battle against AI content, which still finds its way into users’ feeds even when the settings that restrict AI-modified content, which the company introduced in 2025, are enabled.
Putting a similar set of tools into parents’ hands is at least a good first step in allowing the users themselves to dictate the type of experience they want to have on the app.
The new feature arrived alongside other parental controls, including one to stop auto-playing videos and another that lets parents adjust the volume of push, browser, in-app, and email notifications. The Parental Controls Page was also redesigned to make it easier to find and configure certain controls and to allow parents to configure settings related to personalized ads.

Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
16:01:24 UTC
01:01:24 KST

Millions of bitcoin are probably lost for good. Almost none can be proved gone
Estimates put the lost coins at 2.8 to 3.8 million. Only a sliver can be shown to be gone; the rest is a landfill, a password and a guess.
About 20.1 million bitcoin have been mined so far. A good share of them will probably never move again.
In 2017 the analytics firm Chainalysis estimated that between 2.78 million and 3.79 million BTC were already lost, Fortune reported. That was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time.
It is still the figure most reports quote, and it rests on assumptions. A coin that hasn't moved in ten years might be lost, or its owner might just be patient. The blockchain can't tell the difference.
The coins nobody has touched since 2010
The biggest pile of unmoved bitcoin is also the oldest. In 2013 the researcher Sergio Demian Lerner spotted a pattern in the earliest blocks that points to a single miner, since nicknamed "Patoshi".
He estimates that miner earned about 1.1 million BTC, and almost none of it has ever been spent, Cointelegraph reports. Many people assume the miner was Bitcoin's creator, Satoshi Nakamoto. Lerner himself says that can't be proved. Whether those coins count as lost depends on who is counting. That one choice moves the estimate by about a million.
A hard drive in Newport
In 2013 James Howells threw out a hard drive holding the keys to 8,000 BTC. It ended up in a landfill run by Newport City Council in Wales, according to Wikipedia's account of the case.
For more than a decade he asked to dig for it. The council refused, the High Court dismissed his claim in January 2025, and the Court of Appeal refused to let it go further that March. The drive is still in the ground.
Eight wrong guesses
Stefan Thomas, a programmer, was paid 7,002 BTC in 2011 for making an explainer video about bitcoin. He kept the keys on an encrypted IronKey drive and lost the paper with its password.
The drive allows ten tries before it encrypts its contents for good. He had used eight, Cointelegraph reported in 2021, and later reports still describe him as having two left.
The vault that wasn't
Some "lost keys" stories turn out to be something else. When Gerald Cotten, the founder of the Canadian exchange QuadrigaCX, died in December 2018, the exchange said its customers' crypto sat in cold wallets only he could open.
A 2020 staff review by the Ontario Securities Commission found otherwise. It said most of the shortfall came from fraud by Cotten, rejected the idea that the money was locked in cold wallets nobody could open, and put clients' losses at at least C$169 million.
Read more: Was FTX a Ponzi scheme from the beginning?
Burned on purpose
Some bitcoin is lost on purpose. Coins sent to an address like 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE can never be spent, because nobody holds a key for it. People use addresses like this to "burn" coins in public.
Even the first block has some. The 50 BTC reward in the genesis block can't be spent because of a quirk in Bitcoin's original code, according to the Bitcoin Wiki. Coins like these are the only ones anyone can prove are gone, and they are a tiny share of the total.
A supply nobody can count exactly
Bitcoin's 21 million cap is fixed in its code. Supply passed 20 million in March 2026, The Block reported, and the last coins will be issued over the next century or so. Lost coins don't change those numbers. They still count as supply, in wallets that will never sign another transaction.
Mt. Gox shows how blurry the line can be. About 850,000 BTC went missing there in 2014, and about 200,000 turned up in an old wallet a month later. Its creditors are still being paid, twelve years on.
So "lost bitcoin" is mostly an estimate, with a few cases that are certain. Everything else sits somewhere between a landfill and a wallet whose owner is just very patient.
Read more: Is CeFi less secure than DeFi?
Frequently asked questions
How many bitcoins are lost?
Nobody knows exactly. The most quoted figure is a 2017 Chainalysis estimate of 2.78 million to 3.79 million BTC, which was 17% to 23% of the coins mined at the time. It treats long-unmoved coins as probably lost, so it is an estimate, not a count.
Can lost bitcoin be recovered?
Only by someone who has, or finds, the private key. There is no central party that can reissue or reverse coins. Coins sent to a burn address, or the genesis block reward, can't be spent by anyone.
Are Satoshi Nakamoto's coins lost?
Nobody knows. About 1.1 million BTC mined in 2009 and 2010 is attributed to one early miner, often assumed to be Satoshi, and almost none of it has moved. The attribution can't be proved, and unmoved coins are not necessarily lost.
Do lost coins reduce bitcoin's 21 million cap?
No. The cap and the issuance schedule are fixed in the code, and lost coins still count in supply figures. They simply can't move, so fewer coins are usable than the supply number suggests.
What is a bitcoin burn address?
An address that nobody holds a private key for, often a readable "vanity" string such as 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE. Coins sent there are visible on the blockchain but can never be spent again.

Ladybird Web Browser/Engine Reaches Alpha (phoronix.com) 14
			
		 	
				The open-source Ladybird web browser has reached its alpha milestone after four years of development, offering an independent browser engine built from scratch rather than forked from Chromium, Firefox or another existing engine. Alpha builds are now available for macOS and Linux, including Flatpak packages and binaries for Ubuntu and Fedora. Phoronix reports:  As for the expected alpha state: "Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won't work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser."

Amazon’s Decart acquisition is a bet on using software to narrow the gap with Nvidia in the AI chip race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
15:51:07 UTC
00:51:07 KST

Jensen Huang’s comeback as Nvidia’s CEO is understandably making waves, leaving people wondering about the longer-term implications of his quick reinstatement and the U.S. government’s active role in his return. But there was another development yesterday that could also matter for Nvidia down the road: Amazon’s decision to acquire Decart‘s tech and its team for a reported $7.5 billion.
The broader industry seems to agree that Decart’s tech for optimizing AI models to run on non-Nvidia chips is worth several billion dollars. Anthropic reportedly tried to acquire the startup in the same ballpark, and Nvidia, which invested in the startup’s $300 million funding round at a $4 billion valuation, was also rumored as a prospective buyer.
Amazon was ultimately the one to pull the trigger and bring on board Decart’s co-founders Dean Leitersdorf, Orian Leitersdorf, and Moshe Shalev and their team, but the company is not interested in the world models they had been working on. At the heart of the deal is the startup’s tech that helps AI models run better on all kinds of chips.
By incorporating the startup’s Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), Amazon is now hoping to extract more performance out of its Trainium chips, as the company tries to turn AWS into a $1 trillion revenue business.
In its announcement, Amazon said it has worked with Decart since 2025 to optimize the Trainium chips. This deal is ostensibly aimed at accelerating that work, which could eventually result in the company offering its Trainium-based data centers, which Anthropic already uses, to more customers. Amazon has already been working to make Trainium easier to switch to.
One way Nvidia managed to leapfrog its competitors was by spending $6.9 billion to acquire Israeli chipmaker Mellanox, which eventually grew to become a core piece of its international manufacturing strategy. Amazon could well be following a similar path.
Annapurna Labs makes for a more interesting parallel than Mellanox, however, as the latter formed the basis of Amazon’s custom chip-designing unit following its 2015 acquisition. Add Intel into the mix, and this becomes a broader story. “Most of the hardware powering the AI wave was built in Israel. Annapurna; Mellanox; Habana Labs; etc…,” VC Eric Reiner observed on X a few months ago.
In an email to TechCrunch, Eze Vidra, co-founder and managing partner at Remagine Ventures, said the deal is “a strong signal for the Israeli deep-tech ecosystem, showing that specialized local talent continues to attract major global players.”
Amazon still has a ways to go before it can make a dent in Nvidia’s near-monopoly on AI chips, but the deal could help the e-commerce giant speed up its efforts. Dean Meyer, a partner at Sequoia who co-led the firm’s seed investment into Decart, said on X that the deal “will be looked back on as one of the most strategically important acquisitions in many, many years.”

The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
15:50:22 UTC
00:50:22 KST

Computer Science > Machine Learning
  [Submitted on 23 Nov 2026]
Title:The KL Divergence Is Never Negative, Except in PyTorch
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence is never negative, yet PyTorch users have reported negative values for years, and the standard advice is to clamp them at zero. The sign is only the visible part of a silent failure. Many machine-learning applications compare nearby distributions, where conventional KL formulas lose accuracy. On 8.5 million inputs with certified references across 18 closed-form KL families and F.kl_div, we find widespread errors in values and gradients on CPU and GPU. Among scalar families in ordinary parameter ranges, over 85% of FP32 values have at least 1% relative error near KL 10^(-7) (FP16: 10^(-3)), and about 30% become negative at smaller divergences. More precision is not the cure: evaluated one precision higher, the same formulas still leave 7--51% of FP32 values significantly wrong for 22 of 23 configurations. Stable closed-form decompositions, compensated arithmetic, and analytic gradients remove over 97% of significant errors in the working format. Strict repairs eliminate significant errors on 7.2 million scored closed-form samples and correctly round all 567 million scored F.kl_div components. The errors affect parameter fitting, Bayesian decisions, identical-start distillation (up to 97% top-1 disagreement), KL-based layer rankings in a quantized LLM, and 19--59% of GPT-2 circuit edge scores. With the repaired code they all but vanish. Code and data: this https URL

Show HN: Brickie – deploy sandboxes in your own AWS account
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
15:48:34 UTC
00:48:34 KST

Brickie lets you run durable sandboxes in your own cloud / k8s cluster.
Brickie sandboxes are built on top of agent-sandbox with custom snapshot/restore implemented on top of object storage. They are designed to be called from @hatchet-dev/sandbox and support the ability to take a coordinated snapshot of agent state. This means that every sandbox call is a retryable and observable Hatchet task.
Each sandbox session is a container with a shell and a workspace and runs in your Kubernetes cluster with flexible runtime support, including Kata, gVisor and AWS Nitro. Every call that changes the workspace produces a snapshot, which can be used to fork a new sandbox or resume an existing session.
Head over to the quickstart guide to get up and running your own Brickie sandboxes with a local Hatchet instance.
Brickie is in beta. Flags, chart values and the wire contract may change before 1.0. See the changelog.
Docs: here
- Hatchet-guaranteed safe retries: Hatchet's durable execution guarantees mean no wasted compute on retries of succesful sandbox operations.
- Immutable and forkable snapshots: Every call that changes files in your sandbox workspace are saved and stored in object storage. They are immutable and forkable from other sandbox processes.
- Fast starts: A warm pool of pods maintained by the provider means small cold start times for new sandbox pods.
- Custom images: Any image with sh and tar can be used to run a sandbox.
- mTLS for all sandboxes: The provider and each sandbox talk to each other over mutual TLS with strict guarantees around certificate issuance, rotation, and usage.
- Resource limits: Each sandbox is backed by a pre-set network and resource limit to cap usage and to protect nodes from starvation.
- Any object storage: Metadata and snapshots can be stored in any S3-compatible store as well as in GCS and Azure.
- FIPS support: By default, the provider runs all of its workloads in FIPS 140-3 mode with signed and SBOM attested container images.
- Extensible interface: Backed by drivers, the provider can be extended to support more backends apart from Docker and Kubernetes.
pnpm add @hatchet-dev/sandbox @hatchet-dev/typescript-sdkimport "@hatchet-dev/sandbox";
const session = hatchet.durableTask({
  name: "agent-session",
  fn: async (input) => {
    const sandbox = await hatchet.sandbox.create({
      id: input.conversationId,
      template: "alpine:3",
    });
    await sandbox.files.write("haiku.txt", "an old silent pond");
    const haiku = await sandbox.exec("cat haiku.txt");
    await sandbox.kill();
    return { haiku: haiku.stdout };
  },
});
// run the session for a conversation; its ID becomes the sandbox ID
const { haiku } = await session.run({ conversationId: "conv-42" });
// later, from anywhere with a Hatchet client
const again = await hatchet.sandbox.connect("conv-42");
Under the hood, brickie uses the agent-sandbox controller and warm pools to run sandbox pods. On top of this, the Brickie provider does a few different things:
- Every brickie sandbox turn produces an immutable snapshot in your object store, keyed by sandbox and Hatchet run ID. These snapshots can be forked into new sandboxes, or used to resume an existing session. On agent-sandbox, state is persisted through a PVC per sandbox, which forces a cold start, while the only point-in-time snapshot is GKE-specific.
- Every call is a Hatchet task, so it is retried, observable, and replayed from its own snapshot. A retried call finds the snapshot it already stored and does not run the command twice.
- The same code path runs on a Docker engine, so the Kubernetes cluster is not needed for development locally.
- Architecture, how turns, snapshots and the store fit together
- Security, trust boundaries, isolation and image verification
- Drivers and extending Brickie with your own
- Wire contract, what the SDK sends and gets back
- Hatchet docs, the task engine underneath
- Contributing and AGENTS.md, the working rules
Pull requests are welcome from vouched contributors, and the first ones should be small. CONTRIBUTING.md explains how to get vouched, what to work on first and how AI use is disclosed.

Wyze’s new window feeder records birds from a camera inside your home

A year ago, Wyze introduced a $35 security camera that stuck to the inside of a window so you could keep an eye on what was happening outside your home without a complicated installation. Today the company announced its new Window Bird Cam, which expands on that idea by pairing a similar window-mounted camera with a feeder that attaches to the outside of the glass. Alongside the kit, Wyze is also launching a new subscription service called Bird Watch, which adds identification capabilities and features that will benefit busy yards.
Wyze’s new window feeder records birds from a camera inside your home
The camera can be easily installed by just sticking it to the inside a of a window, while the feeder mounts outside.
The Wyze Window Bird Cam is available today through the company’s online store for $69.98 and includes the outdoor feeder with suction cups for mounting, a small tray for holding seeds, and a cover for protection from the elements. Wyze is also selling an optional $14.98 accessory called the Window Bird Cam Perch that gives birds a ”natural landing spot right in the camera’s portrait sweet spot,“ plus a fruit fork, suet holder, and a jelly cup to attract more visitors.
By installing inside your home and plugging into a USB power source (using an included 10-foot cable) the Bird Cam doesn’t need a battery, doesn’t need to be weatherproof, and will be well in range of your Wi-Fi network. Instead of the wide-angle view offered by most security cameras, the lens on the Bird Cam is designed to focus at a distance of 4 to 8 inches so birds look crisp while the rest of your yard is softly blurred.
Out of the box, the Bird Cam will detect motion and provide instant bird arrival notifications while 30fps video is recorded locally to a microSD card up to 512GB. You can also watch and share a livestream from the camera through a mobile device. The arrival notifications do have a five-minute cooldown so if you want to ensure you don’t miss any visitors, you’ll need to upgrade to Bird Watch for $6.99 per month, or $69.99 per year. The subscription adds species identification with a confidence score and access to an interactive bird wiki, full-length videos of bird visits stored in the cloud for 60 days, and no cooldown period between notifications.

A training engine for your local model, using your idle compute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
15:03:40 UTC
00:03:40 KST

Install • How it works • Commands • Roadmap • Discord • Website
Use your local model as usual through opencode, pi or any OpenAI-compatible tool. While you work, Songe notices what happens after each of the model's actions: the tool result, the error, your next message. When your agent is quiet, it teaches the model to see those coming. A new version is used only if it passes its checks, and nothing ever leaves your machine.
- Learns from how you work. Your corrections, stated preferences and the tools' errors become lessons for your own model.
- Two kinds of Dreams. A Quick Dream adds your preferences to the model's instructions in minutes; a Deep Dream trains the model itself while you are away.
- Safe by default. A new version is used only if it does better on your own conversations; one click goes back to any earlier version.
- Stays out of the way. Runs only when your agent is quiet, memory is free and the battery is fine, and stops the moment you are back.
- Private. No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Songe never runs your tools.
With uv or pipx (Python 3.11 or later):
uv tool install songe        # or: pipx install songe
songe init
No uv or pipx yet? Either installs in one line:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh    # uv (or: brew install uv)
brew install pipx                                  # pipx on macOS (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install pipx)
Both give Songe its own environment in a lasting place, which its background service needs.
macOS with Homebrew:
brew tap sous-labs/tap
brew trust sous-labs/tap     # newer Homebrew asks this once
brew install songe
songe init
songe init finds your model server and your agents, shows what it will
change, and asks once:
$ songe init
  Models    3 from LM Studio, listed under Songe
  Agent     opencode → Songe models · default granite-4.2-3b-MLX-4bit
  Agent     pi → Songe models · choose one with /model
  Data      ~/Library/Application Support/songe
  Service   starts at login
  Learning  new conversations · starts when idle
  Replace   loaded copy when a better version is ready
Install? (Y/n)
Then pick a Songe model in your agent (opencode lists them as
songe/songe/<name>), and work as usual.
Plain pip, and what you need
pip install songe works inside a virtual environment; outside one,
Homebrew's and most Linux distributions' Python refuse it.
You need a model served locally, and an agent:
Machines without a GPU still serve and record, but do not train. Tried Songe on another setup? Share the result on the testing board.
 your agent ──► Songe (127.0.0.1:7613) ──► your model server
                   │ records what happened
                   ▼
            when you are away: a Dream
   read lessons ─► practice ─► train ─► check ─► use only if better
With auto-dream on, Dreams start when your agent has been quiet for a
while. Or press Dream in the dashboard (songe open). A Dream never just
disappears: it keeps going on the page, or says why it stopped.
How it learns, in more detail
- Reading. Songe reads each conversation for the moments that teach something: your corrections and stated rules, retries, tool errors.
- Practice. For each lesson your model writes short practice scenes in your agent's own tools. Your real conversations are never trained on.
- Training. The model as it was, shown the lesson, is the teacher; the same model with a small adapter, shown only the scene, is the student (on-policy distillation). Earlier skills are rehearsed so they stay.
- Checking. At the moments you reacted to, the version in use and the new one each answer, and a judge compares what they do. The new version is used only if it does clearly better, does not change what already worked, and its answers stay healthy.
Before the first training Songe measures how much your computer can learn at once, and trains on what fits. See DESIGN.md.
What it changes on your machine
- Its data folder: ~/Library/Application Support/songe on macOS, $XDG_DATA_HOME/songe on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA%\songe on Windows.
- A songe/ folder in LM Studio's models folder with the current learned
version. Your own models are never touched.
- One provider entry in opencode and pi, with a backup.
- A background service that starts at login.
Upgrade and remove
uv tool upgrade songe, pipx upgrade songe or brew upgrade songe: the
service moves to the new version by itself in a quiet moment.
songe uninstall stops the service and restores your agent settings; add
--purge to also delete its data and learned versions. Run it before
brew uninstall songe.
Where Songe is going: ROADMAP.md. Ideas and bugs are welcome as issues. Questions and results from your nights go in Discord. To contribute, see CONTRIBUTING.md. Security reports: SECURITY.md.
Licensed under Apache-2.0.

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
14:54:10 UTC
23:54:10 KST

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
November 23, 2026
I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.
The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.
I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).
I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.
So with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port.  The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.
Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.
Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.
How USB 3 and USB 2 Share a Port
Like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:
Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.
- USB 2 (D+ / D-): a single 480 Mbps pair in the center (pins A6/A7 and B6/B7 are shorted together).
- USB 3 (TX/RX): 2 separate high-speed lanes on the outer edge. Only 1 set is active depending on orientation.
- Control & sideband (CC, SBU): CC1/CC2 detect cable orientation and negotiate USB-PD; SBU1/SBU2 (A8/B8) are used by Apple’s 1.2 V debug UART.
This continues to the computer’s xHCIExtensible Host Controller Interface: the USB controller inside your computer that manages both USB 2 and USB 3.x root ports. controller: a single physical USB-C port is actually wired to two independent root ports: a USB 2 port and a USB 3 port.
A standard USB 3 hub chip like the GL3510 is actually just two hubs in 1 package (a USB 2 hub and a USB 3 hub). On my first iteration of the Dongle-Pro, everything ran through that chip even though the dongle’s own MCU only speaks USB 2 Full Speed (12 Mbps) and has no need for the USB 3 speed.
On the Dongle-Pro v2, the two buses are split apart:
- USB 2 (D+/D-) runs into a CH334P USB 2 hub. One downstream port goes to the target’s D+/D- (so DFU mode and any USB 2 device behave just like the Lite), and another goes to the dongle’s MCU (CH32X035G8U6).
- USB 3 (TX/RX) skips the hub completely. Each port’s two lane sets go into a CH9441P 2:1 muxMultiplexer: a high-speed analog switch that routes whichever side of a reversible USB-C plug is active onto one pair of board traces.. Each mux reads its own port’s CC1/CC2 lines to handle cable flip and connects the active lane set to its common side. The two muxes sit in the center of the board, wired straight together through a short corridor with no hub and no redriverAn active signal-conditioning chip that boosts and equalizes high-speed USB 3 traces to overcome cable and PCB insertion loss..
What Could Go Wrong
This sounded like it would work to me on paper, but there were a few things I thought could go wrong:
- Two passive muxes in series with no redriver. Every connector, ESD array, via, and switch adds insertion loss and reflections. I was hoping two CH9441P chips back-to-back would pass 5 Gbps. But hitting 10 Gbps is even better.
- Sharing the target CC lines. On the target port, the HUSB311 PD PHY actively drives the CC lines to send Apple’s SOP” DebugA USB-PD packet framing addressed to a debug accessory rather than a normal device, required for Apple's DFU commands. VDMsVendor-Defined Messages: custom USB-PD packets. Apple uses them to trigger DFU, reboot, and serial debug without touching the keyboard.. The target’s CH9441P is also reading the lines to steer its lanes.
- Host OS behavior. Even though it made sense in theory, I really wasn’t sure if a machine would happily enumerate a USB 2 hub on a port’s D+/D- lines while a separate USB 3.2 Gen 2 device negotiated directly with the same port’s SuperSpeed lanes.
On the Bench
When the boards arrived, I immediately plugged one into my mac, plugged an iPhone into the target port, and inspected the bus with system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType and ioreg -p IOUSB.
Here is what macOS sees on a single physical USB-C port (AppleT8132USBXHCI@01000000):
The raw system_profiler SPUSBHostDataType output shows both sides active at once:
0x01100000 is the USB 2 half of the physical port, and 0x01200000 is the SuperSpeed half of the same port. The iPhone enumerated straight through both passive CH9441P muxes at 10 Gb/s (USB 3.2 Gen 2), while the CH334P hub and Dongle-Pro-v2 MCU enumerate at 480 Mb/s and 12 Mb/s on D+/D-.
Companion Ports
Splitting the bus required one interesting change in the host SDK (restorekit).
On the Dongle-Lite, whatever device you plugged into the dongle always showed up as a child of the dongle’s hub. That made it easy to tell which target Mac belonged to which dongle when you plugged in several at once.
On the Dongle-Pro v2, that breaks whenever the target connects at USB 3. Just like iPhone@01200000 above, a SuperSpeed target bypasses the CH334P hub completely and shows up as a sibling directly on the host’s root hub.
Turns out the OS already tracks which USB 2 and USB 3 root ports share the same physical port and it exposes it directly:
- On macOS, the USB 2 port’s IORegistrymacOS's live kernel tree of hardware devices, ports, and drivers, which you can inspect with ioreg. entry has a UsbProtocolCompanion (3.x) property containing the path to its SuperSpeed twin.
- On Linux, the USB 2 port’s sysfsLinux's virtual filesystem at /sys that exposes kernel devices, USB hubs, and physical port peer links. directory has a port/peer symlink pointing straight to the SuperSpeed port.
So restorekit can still know with 100% certainty which 10 Gbps device is plugged into which dongle.
Cutting the Cost
I originally planned to have a Dongle-Lite and significantly more expensive USB 3 Pro, but that means having to maintain two hardware lines, so if I could cut the cost of the USB 3 version to be comparably priced to the original Dongle-Lite it felt like a no brainer.
After I removed the GL3510 USB 3 hub from the original design, I went through the rest of the board to see what else I could cut:
- SuperSpeed path: HD3SS3220 ($1.66) + HD3SS3212 ($1.55) + GL3510 ($1.23) came to $4.44 on Pro v1 for 5 Gbps. Two CH9441P muxes cost $0.47 total ($0.24 each) on Pro v2 for 10 Gbps. Pro v1’s SuperSpeed chips alone cost more than the entire Pro v2 BOM.
- MCU: Swapped the RP2354A + 3.3 uH inductor + crystal ($1.62) with a CH32X035G8U6 ($0.42), running off its internal 48 MHz HSIHigh-Speed Internal oscillator: an on-chip clock source that lets an MCU run without an external quartz crystal. with no crystal, no external inductor, and a built-in ROM USB bootloader.
- PD PHY: Swapped the FUSB302BMPX ($0.68) with a HUSB311BLA ($0.51).
- USB 2 hub: Swapped the CH334F ($0.53) with a CH334P ($0.31), which integrates the crystal load capacitors and drops two more passives.
- 1.2 V SBU UART level shifters: two 74AVC1T45 translators plus a dedicated TLV70212 1.2 V LDO ($0.79) became two HL2302 MOSFETs and a few resistors ($0.05) wired as common-gate level shifters.
- Unified ESD and passive discipline: swapped mixed USBLC6 + TPD4E05U06 parts for six H5VU25U flow-through arrays (JLCPCB Preferred Extended = $0 feeder fee), and limited the whole board to just three resistor values and three capacitor values.
Running the three BOMs against JLCPCB pricing:
(Parts and Extended feeder fees from JLCPCB’s catalog, excluding PCB fab and placement fees. V2 wins on fab cost too since it is 40% smaller than the Lite and 60% smaller than Pro v1, packing three boards into one 81 x 48 mm panel.)
These swaps resulted in a 72% BOM reduction from original Dongle-Pro while doubling the SuperSpeed link rate from 5 Gbps to 10 Gbps, and a 42% BOM reduction compared to the Dongle-Lite.
Conclusion
If you are building an inline USB-C tool where your MCU only needs a slow control channel and the host just needs fast passthrough to the downstream device, you might not need a USB 3 hub. USB-C gives you two independent buses in the same port.
Next up: A flash drive with USB 3.2 Gen 2 + 2 speeds?

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
14:54:10 UTC
23:54:10 KST

Splitting USB-C: USB 3 and USB 2 on One Port
November 23, 2026
I started building restorekit.org dongles a few months ago at the Recurse Center. They are small inline USB-C boards that sit between a host computer and a target mac. They set the target mac into DFUDevice Firmware Update: Apple's lowest-level recovery mode built into the boot ROM, so even a bricked Mac can be reflashed. mode over USB-PDUSB Power Delivery: the communication protocol over the CC wire used to negotiate power, roles, and vendor-defined commands. without having to touch the target at all, and work with an open-source toolkit for restoring macs without the need for another mac.
The original board, the Dongle-Lite, is USB 2 only. A single USB 2 hub (CH334F) connects both the dongle’s MCU and the target mac through a single cable, while a PD PHYPhysical-layer transceiver chip that encodes and decodes USB Power Delivery packets on the CC wire. (FUSB302B) sends Apple’s DFU commands on the CC line.
I recently learned from timo at Twocanoes that newer Macs support USB 3 speeds for recovery. I obviously immediately wanted to support this on the hub for faster recovery, but the problem was cost. At first I designed a “proper” USB 3 board using a GL3510 USB 3 hub and a pair of TI SuperSpeed muxes (HD3SS3220 and HD3SS3212). It basically doubled the parts count, and BOMBill of Materials: the full list of components and quantities required to assemble one board. cost, required me to increase the size of PCB to ~100 mm, and topped out at 5 Gbps transfers between host and target (USB 3.1 Gen 1).
I really didn’t want to make a board that cost more than twice the Dongle-Lite just to get USB 3 speeds.
So with the 2nd version Dongle-Pro, I tried a kinda crazy USB-C experiment: drop the USB 3 hub completely, keep a cheap USB 2 hub on D+/D-, and route the USB 3 SuperSpeedUSB 3.x's dedicated high-speed TX/RX differential pairs, physically separate from USB 2's D+/D- wires. lanes as a straight passthrough from host to target on the same USB-C port.  The idea being that in theory the USB 3 and 2 controllers on a USB-C are completely independent, and should work simultaneously.
Since high-speed USB 3 is super prone to interference I didn’t really have a choice other than to purchase a view boards and test it out.
Well… I just got the boards in from JLC and… THEY WORK! They establish a full 10 Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection while connecting the dongle’s USB 2 hub and MCU over the exact same port. After some aggressive cost optimization, the 10 Gbps board also ended up cheaper and smaller than the USB 2 Dongle-Lite.
How USB 3 and USB 2 Share a Port
Like I mentioned earlier, USB-C is not a single data bus. Inside a standard USB-C port, USB 2 and USB 3 sit on completely different sets of pins:
Every USB-C port has two mirrored 12-pin rows: A1 through A12 on top, and B12 through B1 on the bottom, so a cable works rotated either way.

The Inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards Highlight the Vagaries of Daily Life

The Inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards Highlight the Vagaries of Daily Life
From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.
Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”
The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at Studio 551 in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to Adam Oxley. “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”
See more on AUSSIE STREET’s Instagram, where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

In a complete U-turn, Nvidia’s board on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as the CEO and president of the chipmaker, just a fortnight after he resigned.
During a meeting before his reinstatement, however, Huang admitted to more affairs beyond the two that have been reported in the news, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Early in November, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair in a letter to employees. At the time, he was ostensibly talking about his relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (not related to Jensen). Later, it was reported that he’d also had a relationship with Nvidia’s VP of health, Kimberly Powell.
Afterwards, Reuters reported that he also had an affair with another employee.
It’s not clear which affairs Huang admitted to during this recent conversation with Nvidia’s board of directors.
Huang’s return was spurred by a personal intervention from the U.S. government, Nvidia’s board said in a statement on Monday, and President Donald Trump apparently called the board to bat for Huang’s reinstatement.
The Wall Street Journal reports that over the weekend, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told Trump and Vice President JD Vance that the Justice Department wasn’t investigating Huang and there was no evidence that he was a national security risk, after which both contacted the company’s board.
Huang received a “hero’s welcome” at Nvidia’s HQ, with several employees applauding his return.

LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
12:40:15 UTC
21:40:15 KST

LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???
This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[1], but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!
Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.
Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.
And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.
This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for me and have my best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.
On the existential threat or tool question, I'm firmly in the tool camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.
- And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. ↩︎

LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you

LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
5 min read
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?
Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.
So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.
It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. cue Nick Young question marks
Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.
So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone???

A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its don't be evil mantra.

Who in Washington owns and trades Nvidia stock
Every disclosed Nvidia stock trade by Trump and 37 members of Congress, around Jensen Huang's resignation and reinstatement.
Nvidia fell 48% from its October high to 20 November, through Huang's resignation and quarterly results. It rose 33% on 23 November, when the board reinstated him, citing input from senior levels of the US government (NBC News).
Trump's trades in Nvidia stock in 2026
28 purchases ($5.1M to $16.7M) and 15 sales ($4.4M to $12M), plotted on Nvidia's daily close. His latest report, released 19 Nov 2026, runs to 24 September.
▲ Purchase▼ SaleLarger: higher valueHuang outMay not be reported yet
Members of Congress who traded Nvidia stock since January 2025
192 trades by 37 members, largest totals first. The latest disclosed trade is from 28 October. Periodic transaction reports only.
▲ Purchase▼ SaleValue≤ $15K≤ $250K> $250KHuang outMay not be reported yet
About the data
- Holdings: Trump's annual report values his Nvidia stock at $12.5M to $58M on 31 December 2025, or 67,000 to 311,000 shares at that day's close.
- If he still held them, he lost $0.5 million to $2.2 million from 11 to 23 November. We can't tell whether he did: his 2026 trades are reported in ranges too wide to net.
- His accounts are run by independent managers, according to the Trump Organization (AP). The reports don't show who decided a trade.
- Trades can be reported up to 45 days late, so November's will appear by early January. We'll update the page then.
- Congress: periodic transaction reports only, including family accounts. Trades in annual or candidate reports, like those NOTUS found for Eric Swalwell and Ritchie Torres, aren't included.

Investigation of Polymarket Insider Trading on the Reinstatement of Jensen Huang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
11:13:55 UTC
20:13:55 KST

Polymarket : Autopsie d'un délit d'initié sur la réintégration de Jensen Huang chez NVIDIA
[!NOTE] Pourquoi cet article et cette analyse ?
Depuis quelque temps, je constate que Polymarket devient un véritable terrain de jeu pour les délits d’initiés, et le climat politique autour de la nouvelle administration Trump rend ce type d’asymétrie d’information encore plus propice. J’ai donc développé un algorithme qui surveille en permanence les marchés les plus sensibles : chaque transaction y est analysée par des modèles statistiques et des outils de traçage de flux on-chain.
J’ai finalisé l’algo il y a deux jours à peine. Dans la nuit même, en voyant l’alerte se déclencher, j’ai mené une première analyse à chaud sur les transactions… avant de voir tomber quelques heures plus tard le tweet de Donald Trump confirmant l’asymétrie. Et vous allez voir que le communiqué officiel de NVIDIA n’était que la cerise sur le gâteau.
Cette enquête documente, à la minute et au hash près, un cas assez probant de délit d’initié sur Polymarket détecté en temps réel.
En résumé : Pourquoi ce cas est particulièrement suspect
Sur un marché de prédiction, rien ne permet d’affirmer avec une certitude absolue ce qui motive un parieur. En revanche, l’analyse des données on-chain met en lumière un faisceau d’indices particulièrement troublant autour du compte ljhggk :
- Le timing : Les achats s’arrêtent en pleine nuit, 89 minutes avant que Donald Trump ne publie son soutien sur Truth Social.
- L’asymétrie du pari : 4 648 $ misés sur une issue cotée à seulement 6,5 %, transformés en 71 518 $ après l’annonce officielle de NVIDIA.
- Le profil du wallet : Un compte Gnosis Safe Proxy créé 81 heures plus tôt, 100 % monothématique sur ce seul événement.
Simple coup de chance ou réelle information privilégiée ? En décortiquant les transactions bloc par bloc, le scénario d’un simple pari au hasard devient difficile à croire.
1 · L’Anatomie du trade : 71 518 parts accumulées en pleine nuit
Entre 02:19:11 et 03:28:20 CET (01:19 - 02:28 UTC) dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 23 novembre 2026, le carnet d’ordres du marché Will Jensen Huang rejoin NVIDIA by December 31, 2026? était totalement assoupi. La probabilité implicite stagnait à 6,5 %, reflétant un consensus quasi-unanime : suite à sa démission du 12 novembre, un retour de Huang avant la fin de l’année paraissait exclu.
C’est à cet instant précis qu’un acteur unique déploie une stratégie d’absorption agressive, découpée en 4 ordres limités successifs :
Le relevé des 4 transactions sur Polygon
Chaque transaction a été retracée. Les 4 transactions ont été incluses dans les blocs sans rejet Registre complet :
[!NOTE] Verdict technique de l’exécution : L’opérateur n’a pas étalé ses achats sur 24 heures pour moyenner son coût. Il a exécuté un achat massif et concentré en pleine nuit européenne/américaine, absorbant 34 % de toute la liquidité vendeuse disponible sur le contrat, ce qui pourrait montrer qu’il a eu l’info quelques heures avant et qu’il n’a pas spécialement eu le temps de l’étaler davantage. Dès son dernier ordre complété à 03:28:20 CET, il s’est totalement arrêté de négocier.
À noter : le compte s’était déjà positionné sur de petits montants sur ce pari dès sa création, mais sans jamais approcher de volumes comparables à ce qui a levé l’alerte cette nuit-là. Cette montée soudaine en conviction renforce encore la suspicion.
2 · La Reconstitution temporelle : 89 minutes d’avance sur le monde réel
Le cœur du dossier réside dans la corrélation temporelle entre la clôture de l’accumulation on-chain et la chaîne des déclarations publiques.
02:19 CET ─── 03:28 CET ──────── 04:57 CET ────────────────────── 14:30 CET ─── 15:40 CET
[Achats]      [Fin Accum.]      [Post Trump]                     [PR NVIDIA]     [Résolution]
  4 648 $       Verrouillé        « I hope the Board... »          Officiel        1.00 $
               71 518 parts       Truth Social                     Wall Street     71 518 $
                     ▲                  │                               │
                     └──── +89 min ─────┘                               │
                     └────────────────────── +11h 02min ────────────────┘
1. Le premier déclencheur : La publication de Donald Trump (+89 min)
À 04:57:00 CET (22:57:00 EST le 22 novembre), Donald Trump publie sur son réseau Truth Social :
« I hope the Board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the Company, and also, for the U.S.A. »
Il ne s’agit pas d’une consigne officielle, mais le poids politique est massif : la mise à l’écart de Huang reposait sur des craintes de sécurité nationale. Le soutien explicite de Trump débloque immédiatement la situation. Le contrat bondit instantanément de 0,065 $ à 0,14 $ dans les échanges de la nuit.
2. L’officialisation : Le Conseil d’Administration de NVIDIA (+11h)
À 14:30:00 CET (08:30:00 EST), exactement une heure avant l’ouverture de Wall Street, NVIDIA diffuse son Communiqué officiel de réintégration. Le Conseil d’Administration confirme avoir voté à l’unanimité la réintégration immédiate de Jensen Huang au poste de CEO et Board Member, précisant avoir reçu l’assurance des plus hauts échelons du gouvernement américain quant à l’absence de risque sécuritaire.
Le contrat binaire grimpe vers 0,985 $, avant d’être résolu et encaissé à 1,00 $.
3 · L’Empreinte on-chain : Ce que révèle le profil du wallet
Pour évaluer si une transaction relève d’un simple pari ou d’un comportement suspect, l’analyse on-chain apporte des indices précieux. Le compte ljhggk présente plusieurs caractéristiques typiques d’un portefeuille temporaire (burner proxy) :
flowchart LR
  EOA["<b>Portefeuille personnel (EOA)</b><br/><code>0x3e0f9ada318fa8...</code><br/>Adresse signataire directe"] -->|Déploiement Safe| Proxy["<b>Gnosis Safe Proxy</b><br/><code>0xdf8616e18da2ad...</code><br/>Âge : 81h · Pseudo : ljhggk"]
  Proxy -->|100% Capital| Trade["<b>Marché Unique : NVIDIA</b><br/>4 648 USDC sur YES @ 6,5 ¢<br/>Zéro diversification"]
  Trade -->|Dénouement| Cashout["<b>Position Résolue</b><br/>71 518 USDC (+1 438%)"]
4 · D’où viennent les fonds ?
En inspectant l’adresse à l’origine de la création du compte Polymarket (0x3e0f9ada318fa8...) sur Polygonscan, on fait un constat surprenant : son historique affiche 0 transaction. Le wallet est totalement vierge et n’a jamais interagi directement avec le réseau Polygon.
Ce n’est donc pas ce wallet qui a directement fourni ou transféré les fonds on-chain.
Le rôle du pUSD et du bridge Polymarket
Sur Polymarket, le fonctionnement des soldes et des ordres repose sur une certaine mécanique :
- Aucun besoin de gaz sur le wallet personnel : L’utilisateur signe ses ordres d’achat hors-chaîne depuis son navigateur. C’est le relais officiel de Polymarket (Relayer) qui diffuse les transactions sur la blockchain et règle les frais de réseau à sa place.
- Le concept de pUSD (Polymarket USD) : Pour négocier sur le carnet d’ordres, la plateforme utilise son propre jeton interne indexé sur le dollar : le pUSD. Ce jeton n’est pas envoyé par un particulier, mais émis automatiquement par le protocole lors d’un dépôt.
- Le contrat de bridge / séquestre : Quand un utilisateur approvisionne son compte, les USDC réels sont déposés dans le coffre de séquestre de Polymarket (Collateral Vault). En contrepartie, le bridge de Polymarket crée (mint) les pUSD équivalents directement sur le contrat proxy unique de l’utilisateur (0xdf8616e1...).
- L’origine des capitaux : Les fonds engagés proviennent très probablement d’un retrait direct depuis une plateforme d’échange centralisée (comme Binance, Kraken ou Coinbase) vers l’adresse de dépôt assignée par Polymarket, d’un autre portefeuille externe via une passerelle cross-chain, ou d’un paiement bancaire direct via le partenaire d’intégration fiat (MoonPay).
Ce montage montre que l’acheteur a utilisé une adresse totalement vierge pour signer les ordres sans laisser d’antécédents directs, en faisant transiter sa liquidité directement par les infrastructures de dépôt de Polymarket.
Conclusion
Sur les marchés boursiers traditionnels, prouver un délit d’initié demande souvent des mois d’enquêtes et de réquisitions. Sur un carnet décentralisé comme Polymarket, la dynamique est différente : les flux financiers et les horodatages sont publics et consultables par tous en temps réel.
On ne saura sans doute jamais avec certitude qui se cache derrière ce wallet, ni si l’opérateur a simplement eu une intuition exceptionnelle. Mais entre l’absorption brutale de liquidité en pleine nuit, l’arrêt net des achats 89 minutes avant la prise de parole politique, le profil monothématique du compte et l’asymétrie totale du trade, le faisceau d’indices reste particulièrement lourd.
Ce cas illustre à quel point les marchés de prédiction constituent aujourd’hui un observatoire inédit de la circulation de l’information.
Sources
- Fiche de marché Polymarket — Réintégration Jensen Huang
- Polygonscan — Contrat Proxy du portefeuille suspect 0xdf8616…
- Polygonscan — Registre des 4 transactions d’accumulation
- Truth Social — Déclaration publique de Donald Trump sur Jensen Huang
- NVIDIA Newsroom — Communiqué officiel de réintégration par le Conseil d’Administration

En inspectant l’adresse à l’origine de la création du compte Polymarket (0x3e0f9ada318fa8...) sur Polygonscan, on fait un constat surprenant : son historique affiche 0 transaction. Le wallet est totalement vierge et n’a jamais interagi directement avec le réseau Polygon.
Ce n’est donc pas ce wallet qui a directement fourni ou transféré les fonds on-chain.
Le rôle du pUSD et du bridge Polymarket
Sur Polymarket, le fonctionnement des soldes et des ordres repose sur une certaine mécanique :
- Aucun besoin de gaz sur le wallet personnel : L’utilisateur signe ses ordres d’achat hors-chaîne depuis son navigateur. C’est le relais officiel de Polymarket (Relayer) qui diffuse les transactions sur la blockchain et règle les frais de réseau à sa place.
- Le concept de pUSD (Polymarket USD) : Pour négocier sur le carnet d’ordres, la plateforme utilise son propre jeton interne indexé sur le dollar : le pUSD. Ce jeton n’est pas envoyé par un particulier, mais émis automatiquement par le protocole lors d’un dépôt.
- Le contrat de bridge / séquestre : Quand un utilisateur approvisionne son compte, les USDC réels sont déposés dans le coffre de séquestre de Polymarket (Collateral Vault). En contrepartie, le bridge de Polymarket crée (mint) les pUSD équivalents directement sur le contrat proxy unique de l’utilisateur (0xdf8616e1...).
- L’origine des capitaux : Les fonds engagés proviennent très probablement d’un retrait direct depuis une plateforme d’échange centralisée (comme Binance, Kraken ou Coinbase) vers l’adresse de dépôt assignée par Polymarket, d’un autre portefeuille externe via une passerelle cross-chain, ou d’un paiement bancaire direct via le partenaire d’intégration fiat (MoonPay).
Ce montage montre que l’acheteur a utilisé une adresse totalement vierge pour signer les ordres sans laisser d’antécédents directs, en faisant transiter sa liquidité directement par les infrastructures de dépôt de Polymarket.
Conclusion
Sur les marchés boursiers traditionnels, prouver un délit d’initié demande souvent des mois d’enquêtes et de réquisitions. Sur un carnet décentralisé comme Polymarket, la dynamique est différente : les flux financiers et les horodatages sont publics et consultables par tous en temps réel.
On ne saura sans doute jamais avec certitude qui se cache derrière ce wallet, ni si l’opérateur a simplement eu une intuition exceptionnelle. Mais entre l’absorption brutale de liquidité en pleine nuit, l’arrêt net des achats 89 minutes avant la prise de parole politique, le profil monothématique du compte et l’asymétrie totale du trade, le faisceau d’indices reste particulièrement lourd.
Ce cas illustre à quel point les marchés de prédiction constituent aujourd’hui un observatoire inédit de la circulation de l’information.

US To Blacklist Asian AI Firm Megaspeed After Nvidia Scandal (bbc.com) 68
			
		 	
				The U.S. Commerce Department plans to blacklist Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed and its subsidiary Speedmatrix over suspicions that they helped Chinese companies obtain restricted Nvidia AI chips. The move follows allegations that a former Megaspeed executive had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while working as a Chinese intelligence asset, although Commerce officials say their investigation into the company began nearly two years ago. The BBC reports:  The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US. The company is mainly a developer of data centers, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang. [...] When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang. Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US. China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

Worshipping at the altar of Brendan Gregg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
10:50:14 UTC
19:50:14 KST

Okay, I am the first to admit that I’m a bit manic with AI. When you are working on a problem that has endless possibilities, it is difficult to constrain yourself to a limited set of features.
Can I just add one more?
I have been amazed at all the fun and useful things that a deterministic VM like Rewind enables. I have been using it to help find heisenbugs, to make profile-guided optimization reproducible, and to make Nix builds bit-reproducible. But the most fun has been using it to understand performance.
Turns out that performance is yet another area where Rewind shines. I have been using it to analyze the critical path of builds.
What is the critical path?
The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in a program. It is the minimum time that the program can take to complete, regardless of how many resources you throw at it. The only way to make a program faster is to shorten the critical path.
If you worship at the altar of Brendan Gregg, you know he spent years turning performance analysis from a dark art into a science. This is a small offering to him. 🤲
I added a new rewind time command to Rewind that analyzes a recording and tells you where the time went and what would make the run finish sooner. You can drill into any part of that answer and see the source lines responsible for it. It’s like Brendan Gregg’s flame graphs but on steroids for the critical path and with a debugger attached.11All the ideas for the command are either inspired by or directly influenced by Brendan Gregg’s work. Kneel before Zod! 
  Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?
Let’s see how it works by analyzing the critical path of a libuv build and test run. The build and test suite takes 78 seconds inside Rewind, and even with 64 cores it still takes 47 seconds. Why?
The usual answer is to look at a CPU profile, and in this case a CPU profile would be almost useless. For two thirds of those 47 seconds, the work the build is waiting on is not computing at all: it is asleep. 💤💤💤
§Where the time goes
Every rewind time starts with two numbers:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The first is how long the run took on the VM’s one virtual CPU. The second is the critical path: the longest chain of work where each step had to wait for the one before.
No number of CPUs makes a run shorter than its critical path, so the gap between the two numbers is all that parallelism can buy you.
The line under the two numbers applies Gregg’s thread state analysis. Here the biggest state is asleep: 23 seconds in epoll_pwait and 8.5 in clock_nanosleep.
A sleeping thread is invisible to a CPU profiler. Gregg’s answer is off-CPU analysis: look at where threads block, not only where they compute.
On a live machine, off-CPU analysis is hard. Linux can trace which thread woke which, and Gregg built wakeup and off-wake profiling on top of that, but you have to be tracing before the slow run happens, the tracing has a cost, and most of the sleeps you capture are noise. Rewind already logs every context switch because it needs them to replay, and now it records every wakeup and who caused it too. All that juicy information is in every recording. 🤤
Here is the whole output for libuv:
$ rewind time 7a29e716
libuv-1.51.0
    78.0 s  elapsed on the VM's one CPU
    47.4 s  critical path: the least it can take on any number of CPUs
            67% asleep (epoll_pwait 23.1 s, clock_nanosleep 8.53 s, futex 100 ms), 33% computing
The critical path by phase

    1.67 s  buildPhase      █
    42.0 s  checkPhase      █████████████████████
     99 ms  5 other phases

    36.4 s     4910  │  ├─ make › bash › lt-run-tests

    2.00 s     5013  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests delayed_accept delayed_accept  asleep in epoll_pwait 2.00 s
    1.62 s     5126  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_watch_dir fs_event_watch_dir  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.62 s
    1.60 s     5103  │  │  ├─ lt-run-tests fs_event_close_in_callback fs_event_close_in…  asleep in epoll_pwait 1.60 s
