Bambu’s five-nozzle P3C isn’t quite the 3D printer I expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
08:41:50 UTC
17:41:50 KST

Three weeks ago, Bambu Lab introduced the state of the art in home printing tech at $2,499 — now, you can get many of its fancy new features for less than half the price.
Bambu’s five-nozzle P3C isn’t quite the 3D printer I expected
Bambu cut a few corners — and motors — to reach that price.
Like that bigger H3C, the new $1,149 Bambu P3C can also swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce much of the rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.
But Bambu cut more corners than I expected to hit the lower $1,149 / £999 / €1,149 launch price today, and I think they made more of a tinkerer’s 3D printer than one suited for either beginners or pros.
Some of the changes were completely expected, like its smaller 256 x 256 x 260mm print area (much like Bambu’s other P-series printers), and that it supports seven automatically swapping tools instead of nine. (Seven is still quite a lot when affordable toolchangers like the $849 Snapmaker U1 typically offer just four.)
But unlike the H3C, the P3C doesn’t come fully loaded, and it doesn’t load itself. While it has slots for seven rolls of filament and up to seven independent tools (including thicker-than-usual 2.85mm filament, or pens, cutting blades, and debossing and foil transfer tools if you want it to double as a Cricut), it only comes with five 0.4mm print nozzles by default.
And while five is still one more color than you’d get with an $800 Bambu P2S Combo, the 3D printer I’d buy for myself, the Bambu P3C’s automated material system (AMS) is the first Bambu has shipped without any motors to automatically load your filament.
Don’t get me wrong: You can still keep five colors of filament ready to go at a moment’s notice, one more than the P2S, by keeping them loaded into the P3C’s five independent nozzles. You can also buy and fairly easily install two more printheads as well, though they cost up to $100 each.
But loading those nozzles is a slow and surprisingly manual process where you have to shove a string of filament down a tube, quite a long distance by hand, after waiting for the machine to preheat each one, and it feels like a step backwards after years using the earlier motorized versions of Bambu’s AMS. Then again, the P3C doesn’t have to spend time and filament purging between colors like the P2S does.
I expect many 3D printing enthusiasts will see $1,149 for the Bambu P3C as a pretty good deal, assuming they haven’t written off the company’s gadgets after Bambu’s open source snafus. Even five nozzles is enough to load all five rolls of Bambu’s “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and white (CMYKW) filaments for color mixing to produce beautiful creations like the company’s new hummingbird test print, which came out almost flawlessly on my first try.
But you should know that color mixing isn’t necessarily a foolproof way to produce some colors, like the brown tree branch that’s supposed to be the hummingbird’s perch, and I’m not looking forward to manually pulling and pushing a roll of brown filament to change that. Bambu says I should probably try a feature called “mixed color sublayer” for better results, and I also suppose I could daisy-chain a normal motorized AMS to one of the P3C’s printheads, as that is a supported workflow. But that’s why I’m suggesting we’re in tinkerer territory.
I asked Bambu about the decision to not include filament-loading motors in the P3C’s AMS system, and here’s part of the statement I got back from spokesperson Karlie Hou: “The AMS 3P’s design deliberately omits the auto‑loading feature as part of the effort to offer premium multi‑head performance at roughly half the price of the flagship H3C system, allowing a far broader audience — hobbyists, small studios, and educational institutions — to enjoy premium multi‑head, multi‑color printing experience.”
The company says it should take around five minutes to manually reload five nozzles. “In the next [software] update, we aim to shrink the total hands‑on time for loading five spools to under one minute,” the company writes, though that seems like a tall order.
Maybe I’ll put the P3C to a year-long test like I did with the P2S, and see how often I actually need something CMYKW can’t do for me, and whether the filament stays dry when left in the printheads for a long time. The question is: What printers should I test against? Are there any upcoming ones I should wait for?

Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
08:33:14 UTC
17:33:14 KST

Back to Blog
Quad9 Service Deactivation in France
(en français)
Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.
We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.
The Summary
We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beIn’s demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.
We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.
This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.
Repeating the Obvious
We object to the core premise of the legal arguments, which is the false assertion that recursive DNS can or should be used as a method to prevent piracy or any other type of content access. Our position is this is not effective or useful, as we have no monopoly on recursive DNS, and anyone can set up their own resolver in just a few seconds (though without the privacy and malicious content protection that Quad9 offers). The courts and plaintiff have not considered this argument and ignore it entirely in the judgement. Their interest is focused on the possibility for us to do what is demanded, even if it has results outside of France, and their interest is not in why that is unjust or unwise or ineffective. So, we will continue to argue with a refutation of our ability to do this accurately without applying French law to all other European nations and the world.
How Our Withdrawal Will Work
There is an understandable focus on how Quad9 is going to block “French users” when we do not collect user information and have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names. We understand this seemingly apparent paradox, so we will expand on it as it is a question that is frequently repeated.
Our geoIP-based method to identify and deny service to French users is inexact. We are aware that our methods to geographically locate users and declare they are in France is quite imprecise - this is inevitable. By using these methods, we will create conditions of overblocking, where we accidentally classify some queries as being from France when they are not from France, and it will also result in conditions of underblocking, where we do not correctly identify some queries as being from France and inappropriately complete those requests even though the user is in French jurisdiction. This imprecision is a core component of our case: there is no legally accurate way for us to determine what queries are from users located in France versus what queries are from users not in France. But we have no other mechanism - it simply does not exist.
These geoIP lists are inaccurate in two dimensions: firstly, IP geolocation data are often imprecise or just plain wrong, as IP geolocation is not an exact science. Mobile operators span national boundaries, corporate WANs split networks across nations, IP addresses are bought and sold frequently, and network operators shift allocations across borders. These are just a few of many other examples of how geoIP association may not be accurate. Secondly, IP location does not necessarily equate to user location, geoIP data only is a guess as to the location of the IP address, not the location of the end user. VPNs may exit in France but have the majority of their users in other nations; corporate users in one nation may egress in another due to proxies or internal DNS service distribution - there is nothing about a query that has any indication of the jurisdiction of the origin of the query itself.
The data is imprecise, but we do not know to what level it is imprecise. So we must work with what we have.
Why Not Block With This Method?
We could apply this same geoIP filter database to selectively block French users from reaching the sites we have been told to make unavailable, but this would corrupt our core premise which is that the DNS is not the right mechanism for this blocking to happen. If we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users - we lose our integrity and still do not have legally perfect coverage, plus we will inevitably apply French rulings across borders into other nations. We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission which is to only block cyber risks to end users and not content. Secondarily, we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us.
By accepting even the smallest of the demands for blocking based on geoIP data, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we accept to play a complicit role in aiding companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint. We would be admitting that DNS blocking is a valid instrument for the piracy problem - it is not. We would be admitting we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not. We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of content filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.
So we accept there will be egregious overblocking/underblocking errors in our blockade of French users but would rather remain steadfast to our stated mission and principles to uphold the integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you receive the DNS as you (the user) expect, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.
Doesn’t Quad9 Already Block Names?
Quad9 blocks a set of cyber-threats on 9.9.9.9 (and secondary IPs) for end users, where the outcome would be an unexpected and harmful result to the end user (i.e., malicious software). Content blocking is explicitly not in that set. Quad9 has subjective editing on that set, as well - if we believe something is inappropriately categorized by our threat intelligence partners, then we can remove it at our discretion. Additionally, Quad9 also offers 9.9.9.10, which has no blocking of any kind - it is entirely open. The demands we have been given would enforce mandatory restrictions on all our service addresses, which then makes our statements of their functionality inconsistent with the reality that would be forced upon us. We will not accept that condition.
The Future Prospects
We take a long range and principled view to the outcome of this case and the others in line. There are unmistakable long-term risks to Quad9, to user privacy, and to potential fragmentation of the internet that are far beyond the current moment. To give in now would start ‘the beginning of the end’ and allow motion towards internet fragmentation that cannot be undone. We accept the risks and the pain that come with fighting where others in similar circumstances to ourselves must bend and compromise in this invisible card game where end users are not even at the table. We represent those users, and our nonprofit mission of public service is aptly unique by not representing any shareholders, products, or other interests other than the end user.
It is especially disturbing to us to be doing this for an issue (piracy) which we believe is not slowed at all by any involvement of recursive DNS, though the damage to the integrity and trust of the global namespace is significant.
We have seen recent articles about extended blocking demands given to ISPs in France of social media or instant messaging sites, which we anticipate would be demanded of us as well if continued. It is quite clear to us the path that is being taken with these efforts: first create the mechanism, then expand the volumes of the mechanism (unconstrained rightsholder editing of the DNS), then expand the scope of prohibitions to other groups and for other reasons until there is effectively no limit to the number of editors or the reasons for DNS names to be deleted from recursive resolution. This contradicts our mission of delivery of trustworthy DNS results, and we believe this potential outcome to be antithetical to a free and open internet.
This is the second legal assault we have faced to see if the DNS can be slowly corrupted - we stood our ground and eventually won in Germany; with the continued community sponsorship and support we hope to win here, too. We refuse to take even the smallest step towards building the machinery of mandatory DNS restriction, and we will not abandon our obligation to the security, privacy, and integrity we have said we will deliver to users worldwide. We deeply regret having to step back from France and hope we will be able to return some day and offer the same unfiltered services that the rest of the world enjoys.
Legal battles like this drain time and resources away from building a better, safer internet. Your financial support is what keeps us in the fight—and keeps our services free and open for everyone. If you stand with us, please consider donating or becoming a sponsor today.

Quad9 pulled their DNS service from France

Quad9 Service Deactivation in France
(en français)
Today, November 24 2026, Quad9 will disable services for French users. This means any query reaching any Quad9 service address will be refused, and no DNS resolution will be successful. Our planned deactivation will be at 09:00 Central European (Paris) Time, to try to give users who are unaware a chance to respond quickly instead of having services down outside of normal business hours.
We are unhappy to have reached this impasse. For those of you seeing this for the first time, see our announcement of this deactivation from one month ago.
The Summary
We have received demands from beIn (a sports rightsholder company) to block various domains they claim to be related to piracy streaming sites, so users in France cannot resolve those DNS names. Currently, the courts have upheld beIn’s demands, and we have faced fines for non-compliance. We are entirely opposed to piracy, but Quad9 has nothing to do with the piracy sites. This is an attempt to force us to be part of an enforcement regime against third parties.
We have a fundamental opposition to using recursive DNS providers as a tool in this or any other content blocking campaign. Putting demands on recursive resolvers has no effect on the origin servers that deliver objectionable content. Attacking recursive resolvers is a futile and counter-productive effort, but that explanation is not understood. The policymakers and courts of France may of course make any determination they wish, even those that seem ineffective or damaging in our view. We wish to remain within legal requirements where it is necessary. We have our own strict views of what we do and what services we deliver. Because there is a mismatch between the case outcome and our mission, we must withdraw from France to remain in compliance with both law and our internal guidelines.
This is a terrible outcome, but it imposes the least amount of harm viewed over time longer than the duration of this case. We understand this will cause harm in the short term: users who do not know of our withdrawal will find our services unexpectedly unavailable. Users who have to move to different resolvers will not be protected by our cybersecurity capabilities, and they may choose to use resolvers that are less privacy-focused than Quad9.

I'm not excited about tech anymore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
07:46:12 UTC
16:46:12 KST

I'm not excited about tech any more. For the longest time I was excited about new devices, new apps, new platforms—all of it. I've gradually lost interest. I don't think I've grown more cynical—I've always been a cynic. Tech is only interesting when it provides value and it only provides value by being useful. Most new tech isn't useful.
If you're a developer, you are—whether you want to or not—staring down incorporating AI into your workflow. Is it useful? It can be. It can also wreak havoc in your codebase and move your team's bottleneck from authorship to code review. Am I excited about AI? No, no, not at all. I'm not excited about an industry that's consumed the entirety of the internet to enrich a handful of people. I'm not excited about an industry that's building data centers wherever it can, sucking up water and power as it goes. I'm not excited about an industry dedicated to deskilling entire professional fields, to devaluing art and creativity, to flooding the internet with worthless slop, sludge, and spam.
I don't care about self-driving cars. I'd rather have folks in a position to make a living driving taxis. I'd rather we invested in public transit and infrastructure.
I don't care about a folding phone. I have an unremarkable phone with a display that works.
I don't want to be recorded in public by your goofy-looking glasses. I don't need VR—the real world is fascinating without a company mediating the experience.
I don't need crypto.1 Money is a store of value that you can exchange for goods and services. Crypto is a bad investment vehicle with a value totally untethered from reality.2
I don't care about your social platform or short-form video. I'd rather read a book or watch a movie. Your social platform is an echo chamber. Your video is unending and uninteresting.
I don't care about your AI search. Your AI search is worse than what it's replacing: it's less accurate, it takes more energy to run, and it provides no benefit to the publishers it draws upon to provide answers. I want to enter a query, get accurate results, and go to the page providing the answer.
Streaming platforms are now effectively cable, just delivered over a different medium. Streaming music means renting your library in perpetuity.
Appliances don't need an internet connection. Appliances don't need a subscription. They just need to work and work reliably. No refrigerator should require a firmware update.
Cars shouldn't require subscriptions.
I don't need to be tracked. I don't need personalized recommendations. I don't need to establish a relationship with a brand. If I need something, I'll do some research and buy it. Every ad, every tracker, every beacon is something new to block.
So, what am I excited about? Well, mostly, things that are boring and things that are stable. Open protocols, standards, and other things that have stood the test of time. I like email.3 I love RSS. I like APIs and integrations. I like decentralized social platforms. I love tools that do one thing and do it well. Examples? I've got those.
- Fastmail: they do standards-compliant email. It's performant and reliable, and they charge a reasonable price.
- Kagi: I search and I get relevant results. The price is fair.
- Navidrome: I can stream my own music and enrich it with plugins and complementary tools like AudioMuse-AI.
- linkding: I save a lot of links. I share some of those links. They all go through linkding. I archive what I save and store the archive in an S3 bucket.
- Obsidian: all of my notes and writing exist as files on my local disk. It's absurdly configurable and even supports alternative syncing methods. I have a theme that aligns with my site's design and a few custom plugins. It does exactly what it sets out to do, and more if you need it.
What else? ActivityPub, ATProto, CoreDNS, Headscale, NextDNS, bunny.net, DNSimple, and on and on.
Do one thing. Do it well. Be useful. Don't exploit people.

Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Russia May Launch Nuclear Weapon Into Orbit As Soon As Next Month (arstechnica.com) 152
			
		 	
				Western intelligence agencies reportedly believe Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit as early as December, "suggesting the country's development of a satellite-killing weapon of mass destruction is more advanced than previously thought," reports Ars Technica, citing German media reports. Such a launch would violate the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while a detonation could create radiation belts that damage satellites for years. From the report:  The orbiting nuclear weapon would threaten thousands of satellites in low-Earth orbit, including military and commercial communications networks like Starshield and Starlink. A nuclear-armed satellite would also put at risk Western military surveillance satellites and human spaceflight platforms like the International Space Station. A nuclear detonation in orbit would be indiscriminate, also knocking out Russia's own spacecraft and Chinese satellites.
Reporting from three German news outlets -- public broadcasters NDR and WDR and the Munich-based newspaper Suddeutsche Zeitung -- indicates Russia's launch of a nuclear-armed satellite could be imminent. The report says Western intelligence agencies, including the German Armed Forces and Federal Intelligence Service, believe Russia is preparing to deploy the weapon in space this year. Several NATO countries have exchanged their findings on the matter.
The nuclear-armed satellite, designated Sputnik-S, has been in storage in the greater Moscow area for years, the German news report said. German Space Command believes the satellite could be launched as early as December. Once in orbit, a nuclear weapon could loiter for months or years, ready for detonation on the command of Russian military forces. The Kremlin dismissed the report. "Given the number of qualifiers like 'allegedly' and 'possibly' -- not to mention the fact that the claims are attributed to some unspecified source -- they are hardly worth taking seriously," said Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

2035 Came Early
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
06:30:33 UTC
15:30:33 KST

tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.
I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
  Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009
I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.
In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.
One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.
It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.
I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev
It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.
  Aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.
In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.
The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.
JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.
Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.
Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.
GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.
Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.
Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list. 
The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈
Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself.
Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯
2035 came early.

India's opposition storms Meta's offices to get its Instagram accounts back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
06:28:04 UTC
15:28:04 KST

India's opposition storms Meta's offices to get its Instagram accounts back
Last Friday, activists from the Indian Youth Congress, the youth wing of India's main opposition party, forced their way into the building housing Meta's offices in Hyderabad, where they ended up clashing with police among overturned potted plants.
The scene repeated itself the same day in Mumbai, with anti-Meta slogans spray-painted on the building's walls and placards burned in front of the entrance, while in Gurugram, near New Delhi, banners demanded the return of the movement's accounts.
Mumbai police registered a complaint against four of the organization's leaders and detained several protesters.
This anger stems from the November 19 blocking of the Instagram accounts of the youth wing's president and of the party official who oversees it. The Congress accuses Meta of obeying orders from the BJP, Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist party, and of restricting, along the way, thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and influencers critical of those in power.
The movement had warned on X that it would storm the company's offices across the country if the accounts weren't reinstated. Promise kept, then. And the method pays off, since two accounts were restored the day after the protests, according to the group's social media chief, who is now giving Meta seven days to lift all restrictions targeting opposition voices.
Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, compared with around 70,000 over the whole of 2025. The government, for its part, issued almost 200,000 blocking orders between March and July, and since February has required platforms to remove flagged content within three hours, compared with 36 previously.
India is also Meta's biggest market by number of users, and this newfound docility looks an awful lot like an effort to protect its bread and butter.
On the BJP side, a spokesperson accuses the protesters of trashing the Hyderabad office and bragging about it on social media. Meta, meanwhile, still hasn't said anything, caught between a government that gives orders and an opposition that kicks down its doors.
Source: The Verge

AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean in Less Than 10 Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
05:15:22 UTC
14:15:22 KST

AMD EPYC Zen 6 vs. Zen 1 Performance: 12.1x Geo Mean In Less Than 10 Years, Up To 133x In AI
This month brought the availability of the new EPYC 9006 "Venice" SP7 Zen 6 server processors. We have seen excellent generational gains with the likes of the EPYC 9686F and EPYC 9996 over Zen 5 Turin CPUs as well as sharply outperforming the competition from Intel and NVIDIA. With the first-generation EPYC "Naples" processors having launched nearly ten years ago, I was curious to quantify AMD's server performance gains over the past decade. So up today is a look at how the EPYC 9996 and EPYC 9686F Zen 6 processors compare to the original EPYC Zen 1 flagship with the EPYC 7601 across real-world workloads for performance as well as power efficiency for some pretty epic gains.
The AMD EPYC 7601 launched back in June 2017 as the flagship of the EPYC Naples "Zen 1" processors. The EPYC 7601 was notable for its time with 32 x Zen 1 cores / 64 threads, 2.2GHz base frequency, 3.2GHz max boost frequency, and 64 MB of L3 cache. On the memory side was eight channel DDR4-2666 memory and for connectivity were up to 128 PCIe 3.0 lanes. The TDP of each EPYC 7601 processor is 180 Watts.
Now just shy of a decade later, the EPYC 9006 SP7 processors have begun shipping. With the AMD EPYC 9996 256-core flagship are 256 Zen 6C cores / 512 threads per socket, 2.55GHz base clock, 4.1GHz max boost frequency, and an incredible 1024MB of L3 cache. EPYC 9006 SP7 processors support DDR5 RDIMMs or up to MRDIMM-12800 memory at 16 channels. There is also 96 lanes of PCI Express 6.0. The EPYC 9996 has a 600W default power rating.
Or for the frequency-optimized flagship is the EPYC 9686F with 96 Zen 5 cores / 192 threads with a 4.05GHz base frequency and up to 5.3GHz maximum boost clock. The EPYC 9686F has a 384MB L3 cache size while also having a 600 Watt default power rating.
Over the past ten years of AMD EPYC there has been incredible architectural advancements too not reflected in the key specs alone such as AVX-512 with Zen 4 and further refined in Zen 5, security improvements to reduce the need for software-based security mitigations, and countless other architectural improvements each step of the way from Zen 1 to Zen 6.
For comparing EPYC Zen 1 to Zen 6, I dusted off the Dell PowerEdge R7425 server originally provided by AMD for EPYC Naples testing at Phoronix. Nearly ten years later, the Dell PowerEdge server with the dual AMD EPYC 7601 processors still fires up and runs reliably. The AMD EPYC 7601 2P was running with 16 x 32GB DDR4-2666 memory, Samsung SSD 860 SSD storage, and other stock components of this Naples review unit.
With the AMD EPYC 9686F 2P and EPYC 9996 2P testing was the Nigeria reference server with 32 x 64GB MRDIMM-12800 memory, and Micron MTFDMBQ7T6THM-1BP1JABDC PCIe Gen6 SSD.
The AMD EPYC Naples and EPYC Venice servers were tested on the same software stack with using Ubuntu 26.10 for a very up-to-date open-source software experience. Ubuntu 26.10 ships with the Linux 7.3 kernel and GCC 15.3 compiler by default.
In addition to the raw performance testing for EPYC Zen 1 vs. EPYC Zen 6, the CPU power consumption and performance-per-Watt were also compared using the exposed CPU PowerCap/RAPL sensors of 2P processor configuration.

Show HN: Genesis Map – Visualize your agent's changes. See where they can break
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
05:04:41 UTC
14:04:41 KST

English · 简体中文
genesis-launch.mp4
Genesis turns your codebase into a business flow map and shows which of your agent's changes are untested or risky. It runs as a skill inside Claude Code and Codex, and works on projects in Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Java, Rust and most other common languages. Python gets the most accurate results.
We gave Claude Code and Codex 10 recent commits from 5 open-source Python projects and asked what a user would ask: what does this commit change, could it break anything, and do the tests cover it? Each agent answered every commit three times on its own and three times with Genesis. Every answer was scored against a reference answer built from the code and its tests before the runs.
With Genesis:
- Changes that tests run but would not catch are flagged about five times as often. A test runs such a change but would still pass if it broke, like the 🟡 stock change in the example below. Claude Code flagged 8% of them on its own and 38% with Genesis. Codex flagged 4% and 23%.
- False alarms drop to about a third, and real risks hold steady. So more of the risks an answer raises are real: 64% instead of 44% for Claude Code, 72% instead of 54% for Codex.
- More of the entry points a change affects are named: the routes, tools and commands that reach the changed code. Claude Code went from 32% to 47%, Codex from 15% to 24%.
Keep in mind that the first row says less than it seems. Most changes in these commits are covered, so an answer that called every change covered would already score 82%. For Codex it is higher on only 4 of the 10 commits. The difference is in the changes tests would not catch, and even with Genesis about a third of those are still called covered. Codex names more entry points with Genesis, but a smaller share of them are right. The sample is small, 10 commits with three runs each, and the answers were scored by language-model readers, not people. Method and full results: change-analysis benchmark.
The quickest way is to let your coding agent do it. Open your own project in the agent and paste:
Install Genesis by following https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GenesisAgentInfra/genesis/main/docs/install.md, then review my latest commit with it and tell me how to open the result.
Or install it yourself. You need uv and Git, on macOS or Linux:
uv tool install --python 3.12 "git+https://github.com/GenesisAgentInfra/genesis#subdirectory=packages/genesis_ci"
"$(uv tool dir --bin)/genesis" agent install --agent claude
Use --agent codex for Codex and --agent both for both. Other agents, updating,
uninstalling and troubleshooting are in the install guide.
Now open your own project in Claude Code. It has to be a Git repository with at least one commit. Then ask for one of two things:
/genesis map
/genesis review main
map draws the system as it is now, so you can understand it. review shows what
changed since a revision (here main) and whether a test checks it. You can also just
ask in plain language.
In Codex the skill is $genesis. When it finishes, open .genesis/out/latest/view.html
in a browser. The summary.md next to it is ready to paste into a pull request. The
usage guide explains the page and the other files.
Say you asked your agent for guest checkout. It built that, and changed three other things on the way. Genesis draws the checkout flow and puts all four changes on it:
These are the labels on the page. summary.md calls the same verdicts not reached,
reached only, unknown and covered; the usage guide lists
both.
Click a step to see what changed there, the test verdict with the note that explains it, and the code behind it:
Your agent does the reading, but it doesn't get the last word. Every step it writes has
to quote the lines of code it stands for, and the Genesis CLI checks each quote against
a frozen snapshot of your repo. If one doesn't match, the whole description is rejected
and the agent tries again. For Python, Genesis also parses the code itself, so a branch
the agent skips leaves the result marked partial in summary.md. When you map a
project, the page also shows "Partial" at the top. A review's page does not, so check
summary.md.
In a review, Genesis finds the changes itself by comparing the two versions of the code, so the list does not depend on the agent. What each change means, its test verdict and its risks are the agent's reading. The CLI refuses a verdict only in plain cases: Behavior checked (covered) with no cited test that asserts anything, or, for Python, No coverage found (not reached) when a test calls the changed function directly. In other languages, whether a cited test asserts anything is the agent's word.
The CLI calls no model, sends nothing anywhere, and never runs your code.
- Python gets the most accurate results, because Genesis parses it. Other languages work too: your agent reads the code and Genesis checks each step against the source, but a path the agent misses is not flagged.
- Test verdicts come from reading your tests. Genesis doesn't run them.
- Risks are what your agent noticed while reading. There is no rule engine.
- Install: requirements, which flag for which agent, updating, uninstalling, and what to do when something goes wrong.
- Use: what to ask, where the result is, how to read the page.
- Benchmark: what was measured and the full results.
- AGENTS.md: for a coding agent asked to install, use or change Genesis.
Questions and bug reports go to GitHub issues. Report a security problem privately, as SECURITY.md describes.
Apache-2.0. Bundled components keep their own licenses, listed in NOTICE and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Want to help? See CONTRIBUTING.md.

New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees On Cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
03:30:00 UTC
12:30:00 KST

New York Bans Subscription and Post-Purchase Fees On Cars (wgna.com) 162
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from WGNA-FM: On November 23rd, New York State Governor Kathy Hochul announced Bill S.9348A/A.10411A. This bill aims to put money back in New Yorkers pockets by prohibiting any vehicle manufacturers, dealers, or third-party providers from charging consumers more money for locked services or subscription fees. This specifically targets newer vehicles that may lock pre-installed features (like heated seats or screen compatibility) behind a paywall or subscription service. This is becoming more and more of a problem as years go by, and consumers have been very vocal against the practice, but this is a tangible step that can be taken to end this practice before it gets too out of hand. [...] The bill will go into effect on February 27th, 2027.  "No one should have to pay recurring fees just to use features in a car they already bought. My office has secured millions of dollars for New Yorkers throughout the state who were charged illegal junk fees when purchasing a car," said New York Attorney General Letitia James stated. "Unfair fees are fueling rising costs, and I am proud to work with Governor Hochul and the legislature to bring costs down."

Zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in beta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
03:15:38 UTC
12:15:38 KST

Zero data retention with Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in beta
Over the past few months, we've been developing Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) for our business customers. EFS provides state-of-the-art detection of sophisticated misuse, while remaining compatible with zero data retention (ZDR): neither Anthropic nor any cloud providers retain enterprises' data.
Since we announced EFS in September, we've been developing it further with over 100 of our customers—including a quarter of the Fortune 100 and many companies in industries with strict rules on data visibility (like healthcare, financial services, and law). Leading enterprises like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe have been evaluating EFS in private beta.
“Enterprise Frontier Safeguards gives us exactly what we asked for: our logs stay in a Wells-managed environment under Wells-managed keys. We keep custody of our data while Anthropic operates the detection. That split is what lets our teams put frontier models to work safely and meet our obligations to customers, employees, and regulators. We helped shape these safeguards because our industry needs them.”
“Where we have regulated or highly sensitive data, having Enterprise Frontier Safeguards with zero data retention will allow us to confidently accelerate our AI deployment across those highly regulated and sensitive client engagements.”
“As a company that runs critical infrastructure, safety matters as much to us as model capability. We need a solution that gives us strong safeguards while allowing us to keep our data in our own account. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards delivers just that.”
“At Stripe, protecting customer data is foundational to how we operate. Anthropic’s Enterprise Frontier Safeguards will enable us to use frontier models with added protection against misuse. It will also let us retain conversation logs in Stripe’s AWS environment, with access and review governed by Stripe’s security controls.”
“With EFS, customers can keep sensitive data in their own environments, protected with their own encryption keys, while still preserving the specialized safety mechanisms frontier capabilities require. That balance, keeping enterprises in control of their data without abandoning frontier-model safety, is critical to broader adoption of advanced AI in security-sensitive organizations like Cisco.”
Now, we're opening up EFS in public beta. In this post, we explain how EFS works in more detail, how it stays compatible with ZDR, and how businesses can join the beta program.
How EFS provides automated safety monitoring with ZDR
Customers who rely on legacy ZDR are protected by Claude's classifiers: our real-time safeguards that screen individual requests to assess whether they might cause harm. But sophisticated attacks generally occur across multiple queries—and any single request might, in isolation, look harmless.
For example, our September threat intelligence report describes an operation against roughly fifty organizations in which an AI agent divided the work of an attack among many other agents running in parallel. It saved the credentials it had harvested between sessions, so that the attackers could easily resume their campaign. Viewed one request at a time, this attack would have appeared as separate, more benign tasks.
To catch attacks like these, we use a second defensive layer, known as automated safety monitoring. This layer looks for patterns of misuse across many requests. Through EFS, Anthropic can provide automated safety monitoring without storing any customer data. Instead, our automated safety monitoring system analyzes data stored entirely on infrastructure controlled by our customers.
When automated safety monitoring finds a risk, it creates a Safety Case for you to review. These cases can be read from your cloud storage or through an API, and can be integrated with security information and event management systems. They do not include inputs and outputs.
Once it's set up, automated safety monitoring can help your team detect intentional misuse that could lead to serious harm (like offensive cyber operations). It can also help detect agents that take actions beyond a user's intentions, such as—in extreme cases—using a software exploit to access an internal database or external system.
Zero data retention and EFS
With EFS, you bring your own storage for storing inputs and outputs. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider keeps a copy of your data once it is delivered to storage you control. This provides you the following guarantees:
- Zero data retention. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider retains your data. You bring your own storage and store your own data. Inputs and outputs are deleted promptly after they're written to your own storage. You configure your own access policies and audit logging, and encrypt safety data with your own keys.
- No operator human review. Neither Anthropic nor your cloud provider personnel access your inputs and outputs. Only automated safety monitoring can access this data.
- We never train on your data. Inputs and outputs are used only for automated safety monitoring, never for model or classifier training.
You can use EFS through the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, or Claude on Google Cloud. When you use EFS through Amazon Bedrock or Claude on Google Cloud (Google Managed), it's operated by your cloud provider, and the end-to-end data flow stays within that cloud's boundary.
You can use Amazon S3 or Google Cloud Storage in your own account for your storage, depending on where you use Claude. Your cloud provider bills you for that storage as usual, including reads, writes, and key operations (plus any applicable network transfer).
Get started
EFS is available on the Claude Platform, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, and Claude on Google Cloud. Support for EFS in Microsoft Foundry is coming soon.
Eligible customers will be notified with instructions on how to get started. Read our developer docs to learn how to set it up, and our security whitepaper (opens in new tab) for how the architecture works, or deploy it through consulting partners like Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC.

Hacking radiators for fun and no profit
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
03:56:41 CET
11:56:41 KST

Hacking radiators for fun and no profit
My flat has a bunch of electrical radiators, branded Acova. They have a remote. Each. Fixed to the wall right next to it. This means I have to get up from my seat to turn a radiator on. Worse, I might have to get to an entirely different room.
Unlike the TV remote, my radiator remotes are not IR (although an IR variant does exist, and was already hacked), but RF. With no other information, I whipped out my trusty RTL-SDR Blog V3.
As is now usual, Claude helped me quickly detect the signals of the remotes, establishing that they use 868.2 MHz. So I got myself a Heltec V3 for that frequency. Unlike my SDR, it would let me send data, in addition to receiving it.
After more poking with the Heltec, I realized that the remotes seemed to use proper cryptography during pairing, and all communications thereafter were encrypted. That meant that trying to crack the exchanges from sniffed data would most likely not work.
So I took one apart.
Promising! Next to the big black square is a connector with 6 pin holes labelled X1. Most likely a debug port for engineers and technicians working on the product.
After identifying the GND pin with a conductivity tester, and failing to conclusively identify the 3.3V pin, I tried the first guess of Claude for the mapping, with SWDIO on the 4th pin from the top and SWCLK on the 2nd pin from the top. It worked first try!
Fortunately, the MCU did not have any protection enabled, so I was able to dump the whole firmware, and to read memory freely. After I installed Ghidra, Claude was able to analyze the firmware to determine the whole protocol, including the cryptography, as well as dump the session key (determined at pairing).
Interestingly, the firmware is labelled “ComfoRF” and bears marks of the Zehnder Group, of which Acova is a subsidiary. It embeds mbed TLS with various cryptographic primitives, but only ends up using AES-ECB, and implements its own finite-field Diffie-Hellman. Also, it has some logic to use a hardware implementation of AES available on a different variant of the MCU.
With this, I could determine exactly what the MCU was sending to the radio chip. However, I could not read and send commands just yet. The SPIRIT1 radio chip does its own transforms to make the transmission more reliable (FEC, interleaving, whitening), before 2-GFSK modulation. These steps are only partially documented and specific to the SPIRIT1. To use my Heltec module, I would need to know exactly what these steps do.
What I did have were the exact contents of messages going into the radio (read from the MCU using SWD) and of messages going out of the radio (captured using the Heltec). After collecting a few samples, I turned it into a math problem for Opus 5.5, which eventually managed to determine the exact transform used in the SPIRIT1. The real (also generated) prompt was longer, but in essence:
The task. A black-box deterministic function F maps an input byte-string X to an output. I observe pairs (X, Y) where Y is a fixed 64-byte window onto F(X) — the full output may be longer; only the first 64 bytes are seen. Recover F well enough to invert it: given Y, recover X. Approach it however you like; form your own model before reading "What I ruled out."
Data.
- pairs.txt — 5 labelled examples (<input_hex> <output_hex>): input is the full 57-byte record, output the 64-byte window.
- outputs.txt — 1831 unlabelled output windows from the same system.
Observations (verified on the data).
1. Fixed additive mask: Y = M XOR T(X), with M a fixed position-indexed sequence. XORing two outputs cancels M, and the zero runs line up with where the two inputs are equal.
2. Partially linear over GF(2): in some regions Y_i XOR Y_j depends only on X_i XOR X_j; in others it doesn't — so T isn't globally linear.
3. Input-independent invariant block: output bytes 12..27 are identical across every example, even though the inputs differ there. The central anomaly.
4. Leading correspondence: output 0..7 tracks input 0..7, degrading further in.
What I ruled out (read after forming your own view). Modelling T as a GF(2)-linear expansion plus the additive stream M and searching exhaustively: best ~73% of bits, never exact. Observation 3 can't come from a linear expansion, so a non-linear or block-structured component is involved — don't re-tread the linear-only family.
The Claude-generated description of the whole protocol is available in a separate article.
And now the fun begins. I added a separate tab to my TV control panel, dumped the session key of all remotes, and can now control all radiators from my computer, or even my phone. I can even do it remotely, to come back to a warm home!
It took more effort than taking control of the TV, both from me and from Claude, but it worked out in the end. Without Claude, such a project would have likely taken me dozens, if not hundreds, of hours, but it only took about 9 hours of my time, all included.
Now I just need to find a way to control the weather…

Making a dumb TV just smart enough
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-24
03:46:54 CET
11:46:54 KST

Making a dumb TV just smart enough
I own an old, cheap TV. It has no Internet connection, no fancy smart features that make you want to install a Pi-hole, and no ask-me-again-later updates.
However, it is connected to my own desktop computer through an HDMI cable, so I can watch movies and TV series from the couch. Setting it up used to involve going to my desk, enabling the secondary monitor, opening the relevant application, moving its window to the secondary monitor, setting it in fullscreen, going back to the couch, remembering I forgot my wireless keyboard, getting off the couch, grabbing my wireless keyboard, going back to the couch again, and then pressing the Space bar.
The most important quality of a programmer is laziness.
So, of course, I vowed never to get off the couch unnecessarily. And that meant controlling everything from the TV remote.
So, I got myself an IR transmitter and an IR receiver to tinker with:
Then, I fished out an ESP32-C3 Mini devboard, a mini-breadboard, and a handful of jumper wires, and made the most basic device that could solve my woes:
I have played around with Espressif MCUs before, including for early versions of the OmniMorse, but I must admit that Claude is just faster at it than I am. With the help of Opus 5.5, I identified the RC-5 IR codes for each remote button, and set up a few scripts so that a single button press on the remote would do the whole dance I described above.
Problem solved!
But this first success unlocked much more.
I also own a bunch of old consoles. Getting everything hooked up is a chore, and makes a mess of wires. It would be much simpler to run an emulator on my computer and show it on the TV.
Thus, I installed DuckStation, PCSX2, Dolphin, Cemu and ES-DE, configured two Xbox controllers on each of them, and got Claude to start everything from a single button on the remote.
At this point, I was using two of the four colored buttons of the TV remote. So, of course, I had to come up with two more modes. I got Claude to add a Fireplace mode, which just plays 10-hour videos, the most important one being a fireplace. And also Steam, in Big Picture mode.
Soon, there were regular issues with windows opening on the wrong screen, so I switched approaches. Instead of a large desktop on two screens, I resorted to multiseat, which I had always wanted to use, with two separate X sessions, one on each screen. This also allows using both screens at the same time without interference.
But that did mean I could not directly control the windows on the TV from my regular session. So, again, I got Claude to make me an admin panel:
The virtual TV remote actually works, by sending directly through the device I cobbled together. The device also tracks volume being changed from the real remote, so things stay in sync. The rest is just commands to my computer, including a virtual gamepad, and a real-time stream of what is being displayed (mouse clicks work too!). Also, turning on an Xbox controller switches to the emulator or Steam mode, and turning the last one off goes back to the fireplace.
Last, but not least, I took a significant amount of time making (telling Claude to make) everything fast. The whole thing took me about 10 hours in total, most of which was setting up console emulators.
Claude still needs to be kept on a tight leash: it sometimes wanted to go in the wrong direction, left obvious bugs, or suggested fixes that did not address the root cause. However, it saved me a bunch of time on the original problem, and lowered the effort enough to go above and beyond!

Declare is a UI language for you and your AI

Just as SQL is a domain-specific language for database queries, Declare is a DSL for user interfaces — for taking the custom, fluid experience you have in mind beyond a prototype, into a real app: structured, verifiable, and with the design written plainly in its code.

Declare was designed first for the people who make interfaces. Layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are the language itself, not libraries bolted on — so the experience you have in mind is something you can write down directly, and read back later as it was meant.

In Declare, yes. A small language gets it started; these four tools let it catch its mistakes, fix them, and finish.
One installable skill: the language, the library, the conventions, the working loop — nothing to reconstruct from a repository. And declare-help answers any name or error code on demand.
Every diagnostic names the broken rule and the valid rewrite. Try it: change textColor to color in the panel above and read what comes back.
The Inspector can tell you or an agent why a live value is what it is, what it depends on, and what happens if you change it — live, in the running program, not guessed from source.
A formal six-rung ladder, from parse to pixels, is how an app is shown to be correct. Your AI climbs it one rung at a time, and every rung reports what it proved — and what it cannot see.
Measured: given the same brief, the same agent built a ticket-buying app twice. The Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark — every run is in the repository.
The calendar above was built this way: human-designed and directed, built with AI, and kept honest by the compiler.

WHY DECLARE
Start with the obvious objection. AI writes most code now, and it is best at the languages it has seen the most — so the sensible move is to use whatever has the biggest corpus and let the model figure it out. By that logic the era of new programming languages is over.
That argument gets its facts right and its conclusion backwards. Writing code is now nearly free; trusting it costs what it always did. An AI writing React verifies its work by resemblance — this looks like the billion lines it trained on — and resemblance is not correctness. Meanwhile less and less code passes under human eyes, which leaves the language and its compiler as the one reviewer that is always present. Handing the writing to a machine doesn’t make the language irrelevant. It makes it load-bearing.
Declare set out to be two things at once.
Expressive. A language that can say what a real interface is — not just data entry screens, but fast, polished, custom software designed to be used, even enjoyed: views that become the next view, motion that carries meaning, layouts that answer to content and to the screen they are on.
Verifiable. A language that can be learned, written, debugged and tested by an AI, and whose programs a compiler can check rather than guess at.
Most attempts to make code safe for machines make it duller for people. Declare refuses that tradeoff. Every feature that makes a program checkable — one tree for structure, style and behavior; every dependency visible to the compiler; one decider for each value — is also what makes it short, and readable to the person who has to judge it.
A well-designed experience is a set of decisions — how it should look, how it should move, what should feel inevitable — and those decisions are yours. An AI can produce a standard-looking app easily, and in Declare it can produce one verifiably. What it cannot supply is a custom-crafted design.
That is why layout, motion, states, theming and drawing are part of the language itself rather than libraries: a Spring on an attribute, a layout as a value a view holds, a mode as a state you are in or not. The continuous version of an interface is often less code than the discrete one. And because a Declare program is one complete description — no separate stylesheet, no framework lifecycle, no build of a dozen files — the design you meant is written plainly in the code, where you, a colleague or an AI can read it back and see that it is still what you meant.
What an AI gets from a mainstream stack is corpus leverage: fluency by imitation — broad, shallow, self-contradictory, unverifiable. The other kind is comprehension leverage: a language small enough to hand to a model whole, regular enough that its programs can be analyzed rather than pattern-matched, and backed by a compiler that turns each mistake into a precise correction. Corpus leverage arrives free with popularity. Comprehension leverage has to be designed in, and it is the only kind a new language can compete on.
It is a measured bet: a small language handed to a model in context has beaten the same model writing Python (study →), and a compiler that explains its errors measurably improves a model’s repairs (study →).
Declare was built the same way it is meant to be used: eval by eval. An agent that had never seen the language was given a written application spec and the Declare download, and built the app while I watched — how long it took, what it tripped on, what it found missing, how well its code read, how well the app worked. Another agent built the same spec in React. Over a hundred runs, what improved was not the model but the language: the same ticket-buying app went from 48 minutes to 24, compiler errors per build from 32 to 6. In the latest pair the Declare app was 1,279 lines to React’s 2,666, and its first build that ran passed all eleven hidden checks; React’s passed six. Single runs, not yet a benchmark. The runs, in full →
The most prized quality of a great interface — the continuity you feel in the best native apps — has always been bespoke: specialist craft, one interaction at a time, locked to a platform, and wrong in ways nothing catches. Declare makes that continuity the grain of the language, and puts it where a compiler can check it. The calendar is the proof: four views as one zooming surface, about 600 lines, human-designed and directed, and built with AI.
There is another generation of experiences beyond today’s hand-crafted best — built on a foundation with continuity at its core, deployed as widely as a URL, and shaped by people with an idea of how software should feel, working with an AI at their side. Declare is built to find out what they make.
Further: the FAQ · how it works · the whole language, in one file
WHERE THIS CAME FROM
I co-founded Laszlo Systems and led the team behind OpenLaszlo — a declarative UI language, first shipped in 2002, that pushed right to the edge of what that era’s web browsers could handle.
What brought me back to UI development was Mesa, a zoomable canvas app I built without using a browser framework, toolkit, or higher-level language. Mesa renders a thousand live objects at a 60fps floor, even on a phone. It’s been positively amazing to see how fast today’s browsers have become — and how powerful and flexible today’s web platform is.
And yet the web as it actually stands is still, mostly, slow and clunky. Even brand-new sites. How can that be?
It turns out the browser isn’t what makes the web feel worse than a good native app. It’s what we’ve built on top of it. A lot of accumulated code — and a lot of accumulated habits — take their toll, and the interfaces that do escape them are hand-crafted, one at a time, by specialists.
In June I handed the original OpenLaszlo compiler to an LLM and got back a modern port that compiles any OpenLaszlo program perfectly, byte-for-byte.
Seeing those programs again through fresh eyes — and seeing how small and how fast the sites built with them are — I decided the language deserved to be modernized. Declare is what came out of that: a direct descendant of OpenLaszlo, with the core ideas intact, built on an entirely new foundation, and shaped to be written with an LLM.
Enjoy!
— David Temkin
THE LANGUAGE
Declare is a language for building application interfaces. This file is the language: every form the grammar accepts and every rule the compiler enforces. The compiler completes it — every error carries a code, a position, and the rewrite that resolves it (§12), so nothing here needs to enumerate edge cases.
Declare is new, and no LLM has been trained on it. It resembles React, CSS, and HTML in places, and this file is where those resemblances stop. Every complete program below is compiled by the test suite, so the examples are current by construction; where this file and the compiler disagree, the compiler is right.
The classes and their attributes are in the reference — npx declare-help <name> answers any of them by name. How to work with Declare, and where everything else is, starts at skill/SKILL.md.
One boundary makes the rest of this file readable. Every capitalized tag is a class — View, Text, and Image, but equally Dataset, State, Spring, and KeyListener. The language is the grammar that declares, instantiates, configures, and relates them, and that grammar is what follows.
A Declare program is a tree of nodes whose attributes are related to each other by standing expressions the runtime keeps true.
A constraint is a relationship, not a callback. Read a reactive value inside one and you are subscribed to it; assign to that value and everything that reads it updates. There is no re-render, no diffing, no dependency array, and no hook, because nothing was ever a render.
App [ width = 400, height = 140, fill = darkslategray, textColor = whitesmoke,
    count: number = 0,                               // reactive state
    col: View [ x = center, y = center,
        layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = y, spacing = 14, align = center ],
        Button [ label = "Add one", primary = true, onClick() { app.count = app.count + 1 } ],
        Text [ text = { `Clicked ${app.count} times` } ]
        ]
    ]
Click the button and the label updates; resize the window and it stays centered. You wrote no update logic for either, and there is nowhere to put any. Every section below is this same idea applied to structure, space, data, style, and time.
{ } is TypeScript, and only TypeScript. Bare values have their own literal vocabulary, and it stops at the brace: width = { 100% } is a syntax error, and a color inside braces is "#4169E1" or 0x4169E1, never bare #4169E1. (§2)count = count + 1 sets and notifies. There is no setState, no setAttribute, and no way to change a value without the cascade. (§5)[ ] tree never generates children from an expression, so React's {items.map(…)} and {cond && …} have no equivalent there: a collection comes from replication over a datapath, and conditional presence is visible. (Both are ordinary TypeScript inside createView, just not in the tree.) (§7)app.width. The renderer makes what the browser's own features need (the tree a screen reader reads, the fields autofill fills) from what you declare: a role, a name, a purpose. Its elements are not an interface. (§6, §9)provided(…) finds the nearest value an ancestor provides (§9), and a key the nearest binding a view declares (§8).onLoad, onArrive, afterSettle). Time is only ever an input — a duration to animate over, a frame step to integrate by. (§5, §10)
Two brackets carry the entire syntax. [ … ] holds a node's members — attributes, declarations, methods, children — and the bracket nesting is the tree. { … } is TypeScript, type-checked against every class's real API.
An attribute's value takes four forms, and the spelling tells you which:
A bare literal is the value itself, so a name is not one: fill = accent fails as a bare value. Reach a named value through braces — fill = { provided("theme").accent }.
Bare values have a small literal vocabulary the compiler owns: Lengths (100%), colors (navy, #336699), and keywords (center, x). Inside { } none of it exists. You are in plain TypeScript, an identifier means what TypeScript says it means, and the compiler never reinterprets it.
fill  = cornflowerblue,                           // ✓ bare value, a named color
fill  = { hovered ? 0x6495ED : 0x4169E1 },        // ✓ in braces, TypeScript number
fill  = { hovered ? #6495ED : 0x4169E1 },         // ✗ no such syntax in TypeScript: "#6495ED"
width = 100%,                                     // ✓ bare value, Length literal
width = { 100% },                                 // ✗ compute it instead:
width = { parent.width - 40 }                    // ✓
A body is TypeScript, written as TypeScript writes it: ternaries, template literals, array chains, closures, casts (x as T, x!), annotations on locals and parameters, generics, and a method body's own type, interface, enum and class declarations. Everything type-level is checked, then stripped; what TypeScript compiles (an enum, a class's parameter properties), the compiler compiles. One limit, a compile error naming the rewrite: a value body is a single expression — statements live in methods.
A :path may also appear inside a { } body, and this is central rather than exotic: it is how anything conditional over replicated data gets written. text = { :on ? :title : "—" } reads the datapath exactly as the bare form does, then computes with it in TypeScript. Read { } as "TypeScript, plus datapath reads."
Two lexical notes. A "…" string ends at its line, in a bare value as in a { } body; a """ block is the form for long text. And a Dataset's literal body is strict JSON (§7) — the one place { } is not TypeScript at all.
Everything inside [ ] is a member, in one of five shapes. Two of them look nearly identical and mean different things.
width = 100%,                          // SET an attribute that already exists
x     = { parent.width - 40 },         // SET it live — a constraint
text  = :title,                        // SET it from bound data
label:    string  = "",                // DECLARE a new reactive attribute
selected: boolean = false,
tint:     Color   = navy,              //   any value type, bare-literal default
count:    number,                      //   no default — undefined until written
rows:     number[] = [],               //   an array, element-typed
panel:    Menu?   = null,              //   a class — the attribute holds an instance, or null
select() { selected = !selected },     // a METHOD
onClick()      { count = count + 1 },  // a HANDLER — `on` + an event this node fires
onPointerMove(e: PointerEvent) { x = e.x },   // pointer handlers get a typed payload
draw(d: DrawContext) { d.fillStyle = "#4169E1"    // a METHOD the view calls to paint itself — see below
            d.fillRect(0, 0, 12, 12) },
bg: View [ fill = midnightblue ],      // a CHILD, named — reachable as `bg`
Text [ text = "OK" ]                  // a CHILD, anonymous
Any view can paint itself by defining draw(d: DrawContext) — graphs, gauges, iconography, marks no fill or font gives you. It is an ordinary method: View calls it from a constraint of its own (drawing = { record(draw) }), so it runs on invalidation and re-runs when what it read changes, never per frame — the same rule as any method a constraint calls. d takes the Canvas2D drawing calls (fillStyle, beginPath, moveTo, stroke, …); what it records, every renderer paints.
name = value sets an attribute that exists; name: Type = value declares a new one. Declaring is how reactive state enters a program; setting is how it is wired. A declaration's type is a TypeScript type — number, string[], "idle" | "busy", Map<string, Row>, { x: number; y: number }, [number, number], (id: string) => void, Row | null — naming TypeScript's built-ins, Declare's own (Color, Length, …), your classes, your schemas (§7), or a type a script block declares; object / array stand for a record or list of no declared shape, in a cast too. T? is Declare's shorthand for T | null, and takes ?.'s undefined as null. A type that a declaration cannot hold in place (a conditional or template-literal type) is named once in a script block and used by name. The one place a type meets the member syntax is a [ after it: glued and empty it is an array (w: Window[]); after a space it opens a named child (w: Window [ … ]).
A method's signature is typed, name-first: select() { … }, commit(v: boolean) { … }, quant(v: number) -> number { … }. Every parameter carries a written type — any type a declaration takes, an event payload among them (onPointerUp(e: PointerUpEvent)); c?: Menu, or Declare's c: Menu?, says the value may be absent, and the body must check. The return is written -> Ret or TypeScript's : Ret — a type's name (-> Week, -> Session[]), not a record written out in place: give a returned record a schema and return that. Omit it for a method that returns nothing. A computed value is still not a method but an attribute with a { } default, segIndex: number = { … } — an attribute stays reactively true; a method runs when called. A subclass's method, handlers included, replaces the base's of the same name, a built-in's own runtime methods (fetch, start, scrollTo) among them; super.name(args) calls the replaced one, wherever in the body it is written, or never.
Events from outside the tree come through a member you declare. KeyListener [ onKeyUp(e: KeyEvent) { … } ] hears the raw keyboard regardless of focus. There is no subscription syntax and nothing to unregister: the source is a child, so it lives and dies with the node that declares it.
Members are separated by commas; a trailing one before a closing ] is legal.
A bare name resolves outward through the enclosing brackets, innermost first — the brackets are the scope exactly as they are the tree. Each [ ] you are nested inside is a level whose surface is that node's whole member set, and the nearest level owning the name wins, at compile time. One consequence to hold on to: every view carries the built-in attributes, so a bare width always means this node's width — built-ins never resolve outward.
Three reserved words say it explicitly, and nothing else may take their names: this (the node the code is written on), parent, and app (the running application, from any depth — the home of the few values the whole app shares). Bare App is the class; app is the instance. A fourth, classroot, belongs to authoring a class and arrives in §4.
Every name the platform adds is capitalized: a class, a type with its builders (Stroke(1, red), Color.mix(a, b, 0.5)), a service (Focus), or a theme preset. A lowercase name is yours, the node's or JavaScript's, besides provided, measureText and escapeHtml.
A member is a property of its view, reached as JavaScript reaches one: toolbar.share, or by a name computed at run time, toolbar[name]; the two chain freely. Each bracket steps one level and names one member, else undefined. A literal name is checked like a path; one known only at run time cannot be.
Instantiate a class by naming it with a [ ] body; define one with class Name [ … ]. A class with no base is a view; any other base is named — extends Node for a class with no view, extends Dataset for a class with no view that holds data (a Dataset is a Node), extends Control or any class of yours or the library's.
class Chip [ height = 30, cornerRadius = 10, fill = darkslategray,
    label: string = "",
    width = { this.t.width + 20 },
    t: Text [ x = 10, y = 5, fontSize = 12, text = { label } ]
    ]
App [ width = 400, height = 100, fill = black,
    layout: SimpleLayout [ axis = x, spacing = 10 ],
    Chip [ label = "one" ],
    Chip [ label = "two" ]
    ]
App is the one root, one per program; with width and height unset it fills its host. Any instance may declare its own members — state, methods, handlers — with no class at all, because the compiler synthesizes an anonymous subclass, and the instance remains a subtype of its base. Promote a one-off to a named class when you instantiate it twice, or when pulling it out keeps its parent readable. The same holds for what has no view: state and logic can live on the App, and when a group of it becomes a thing in its own right — the rules of one dataset's records, a service, a piece of machinery — it moves into a class of its own that extends Node, or Dataset when it is those records' own logic.
A subclass adds children; defaultPlacement says where they go. A subclass's children (and a use site's) are appended to the instance, after the base class's own. A class that is a frame around content names the child the content belongs in — class Sheet [
defaultPlacement = body, body: View [ … ] ] — and every subclass's and use site's children go into body, in order, and a layout: written with them goes too, arranging them there; the base's children keep its layout. A child can exist conditionally: exists = { … } builds it while true and discards it while false, in its place (visible keeps a hidden view built — a focus sink, a definition read by its parent).
Besides class, the top level holds script, include, use, theme, style, schema, ship, defaultFlags and declareVersion — the complete set, in any order, before or after the root instance; extends may name a class declared later in the file. script { … } holds free TypeScript — helpers, parsers, whole libraries — and may import ES modules, bundled at compile; script [ "file.ts" ] is the same block loaded from a file. A program's script blocks share one scope, in source order, and a constraint may call into script, opaquely (§5). A script runs on every host, so it uses only what all of them provide; one written for some hosts says so — script [ host = browser ] { … } — and the compiler refuses an unmarked script's host-only names (Structure). include
[ "path.declare" ] merges another file's top-level declarations, once. use [ Name ] keeps a class the build would otherwise drop, for code that constructs it by name (createView, §7). ship [ … ] says what a self-contained package must carry beyond what its source names (Packaging); defaultFlags [ … ] gives the program's own defaults for the platform's flags, such as render = canvas (defaultFlags); declareVersion [ "0.6.0" ] says which release a file was written for, and no program needs it. theme Name [ … ] and style Name [ … ] are named records of literal values — a token record, and the style of a run of text with no view (§9).
classroot
classroot is legal only inside the body of a class you are defining, and nowhere else — if you are not writing class Name extends Base [ … ], you do not want it. It names the instance itself, from any depth inside the class: the reach for a handler or a deep subview acting on the instance, and the explicit spelling when a nearer child shadows a bare name.
class WeatherTab [ selected: boolean = false,
    label: string = "",
    select() { selected = !selected },
    header: View [
        onClick() { classroot.select() },              // `this` here is the header, not the tab
        caption: Text [ text = { classroot.label } ]  // reaches the tab from a leaf
        ]
    ]
A direct child of the class body can reach the same instance as parent, and that is legal — parent is the enclosing view, which for a direct child is the instance itself. The difference shows up later: nest that child one level deeper and parent now means the new wrapper, while classroot still means the instance. Reach for classroot when you mean the instance, and keep parent for when you mean whatever encloses me.
A { } as an attribute's value is a constraint: re-evaluated when, and only when, its inputs change.
x    = { parent.width - width - 20 },               // stays 20 from the right edge
fill = { selected ? 0x4169E1 : 0x191970 },           // royalblue / midnightblue
